[728] The governance principles are independent of economic and other framework conditions

[729] Smooth implementation of the major restructuring challenges facing the Armed Forces requires a better-defined management and administration system than is currently practiced

[730] The concept defines goal and performance management of the Armed Forces' activities and resource use

[731] It is embodied in four main principles and a management model, which links the use of resources in the Armed Forces to the effects that society expects from the Armed Forces' activities

[732] The four principles of the governance concept are

[733] Clarification of responsibility and authority

[734] Delegation of responsibility and authority as far as is appropriate - Responsibility and authority are followed

[735] Responsibility is asserted

[736] These principles involve uniform management lines and the allocation of responsibilities and the definition of authority in accordance with responsibility

[737] Managers at all levels will be given overall responsibility, including expanded responsibility for administrative functions and greater freedom to manage allocated and available resources in order to meet the performance requirements placed on the business

[738] As a consequence of this, the management lines and the role of the administrations will change significantly

[739] Resource management takes place in two main phases

[740] First, in a long-term perspective through a planning and prioritization phase where it is decided what the resources will be used for

[741] Secondly, in an implementation phase where responsibility for implementing the decisions is placed together with the allocation of resources

[742] This occurs in connection with the annual budget process

[743] Implementation should, in principle, take place by delegating and assigning authority, responsibility and tasks from the top level downwards

[744] Important management tools will be information technology, results management and management dialogue between levels in the organization, and a financial management system that ensures both management and control of spending for the Armed Forces' various organizational levels and relevant levels

[745] Internally within a unit, business planning and preparation of annual business plans will be key management tools

[746] Demand mechanisms will be utilized to the extent that this is found rational, appropriate and profitable

[747] Great emphasis will be placed on achieving the highest possible degree of equality and uniformity within the management and leadership of the Armed Forces' activities in peace, during crisis and in war

[748] The report is structured in accordance with the restructuring and adaptation of the Ministry's management functions that are aimed for both in the short and long term within the framework of the new management concept for the Armed Forces

[749] Adaptation of the distribution of responsibilities and tasks

[750] Restructuring the management and administration of the Armed Forces' use of resources creates a need for changes and adjustments to the division of tasks and responsibilities and clarification of command-related matters for several levels within the Armed Forces' organization

[751] This particularly affects the central management functions

[752] The Ministry of Defence shall ensure that subordinate agencies have an appropriate form of governance and organisation

[753] so that the principles in the Armed Forces' management concept are complied with, see Chapter 10. The administrations and joint institutions are support elements for the rest of the Armed Forces' organization

[754] Based on the principle that resources should follow the missions, the administrations and joint institutions must be given a management and organizational form that ensures overall management and control of them, and provides the necessary freedom of action for management, efficient operation and adaptation of the activities to the needs and activities of the Armed Forces

[755] Security policy perspectives and frameworks. NORWAY'S SECURITY

[756] The end of the Cold War and the development towards a security order in Europe characterized by dialogue, cooperation and community have clearly contributed to increasing Norway's security

[757] The post-war era has ended, a new era has begun

[758] In 1992, there was no immediate military threat to Norway

[759] Nevertheless, there is a high degree of uncertainty about continued developments and a number of fundamental security policy challenges

[760] The previous threat picture based on a division of Europe has been replaced by a new risk picture, based on a multifaceted and unclear European development, with uncertainty and unpredictability as the most important characteristics

[761] For Norway, this uncertain development is primarily linked to developments in Russia, and to the future relationship between Russia and the rest of Europe

[762] However, ethnic, national, religious and social contradictions and conflicts can weaken stability in Europe as a whole and thereby also have direct consequences for Norway

[763] The uncertainty associated with the new situation is due to a significant extent to the fact that Europe is in the midst of a transition phase

[764] The significant changes in international politics are also due to the fact that North America and Asia are characterized by changes

[765] The changes inside and outside Europe mutually influence each other

[766] As a result, not only has the post-war period and the Cold War ended; it is also still unclear what will characterize the international order that may emerge beyond the 1990s

[767] In the current situation, the most serious traditional security policy challenges often appear to be the least likely

[768] A number of new challenges represent political realities that must be addressed

[769] The fundamental political and military strategic changes that have taken place in Europe since 1989 must be considered largely irreversible

[770] The unification of Germany and the dissolution of the Soviet Union, as well as the Russian military withdrawal from Central and Eastern Europe, will have significant and lasting consequences for future developments in Europe

[771] It is unlikely that the Soviet Union or a similar successor state under centralized leadership will be able to re-emerge

[772] Russia will - for political, economic and technological reasons - not be able to maintain military forces to the same extent as the Soviet Union could

[773] The end of the post-war period and the dissolution of the Soviet Union have meant that the likelihood of local or regional conflicts has increased in Europe, while at the same time the likelihood of a major conflict has decreased

[774] This also increases the likelihood of the use of armed force

[775] The conflicts in what was Yugoslavia show that war is still possible in Europe

[776] To prevent such regional conflicts from spreading, there is now a greater need for international cooperation than ever

[777] Developments have also made the question of the use of armed forces for crisis management and peacekeeping or peace-making operations a central security policy issue

[778] In the new situation, such use of military forces has also become relevant in Europe

[779] In the new Europe, the threat to Norway's security will - at least in the short term - not just be a distant possibility of a direct attack on Norwegian territory

[780] It will also consist of threats to the rules, norms and standards that are necessary to maintain at least a minimum of order in Europe

[781] This system of norms has been developed and codified in the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE

[782] Ethnically and religiously based local conflicts can spread, and can also break down the system of norms that has been created

[783] Consequently, Norway, like other countries in NATO, will have to contribute to emergency forces that can contribute to rapid presence in vulnerable parts of the NATO area as well as to efforts in peacekeeping and peace-making operations

[784] Cf. St. report no. 14 (1992-93) Preparedness for peace

[785] About Norway's future military involvement in the UN and the UN's role as a conflict resolver

[786] Developments in Europe since 1989 have made it even clearer that Norwegian security cannot be achieved without security in Europe

[787] The importance of community security is fundamental in this light

[788] The security of no European country can be safeguarded without simultaneously taking into account the security of all other European countries

[789] Against this background, the design of the future Norwegian defense structure and the determination of which tasks and which role the Armed Forces will be assigned will have to be considered in the context of what the Armed Forces are sought to be used for as the most central security policy instrument

[790] The end of the post-war period and the division of Europe means that military factors have taken on a less prominent place in international politics, although they still play a significant role

[791] Full implementation of the CFE-I Treaty on Conventional Disarmament in Europe will help to reduce the importance of purely military factors for security in Europe

[792] Key security policy issues

[793] The right to self-defense in the event of armed attack is fundamental and enshrined in the UN Charter

[794] The need for national military defense stems from the nature of the international system

[795] The function of security policy in a broad sense is to ensure the safety, rights and welfare of the population

[796] After the emergence of democratically governed European nation-states, this has been at the center of the tasks of state power

[797] For small states that have stood alone, the task often proved impossible if larger states with large military resources acted willfully or aggressively

[798] This created a need for common solutions

[799] Because the larger states have also been unable to guarantee the security of their populations in the nuclear age, the situation has changed from the perspective of small states, while both small states and great powers now have an interest in the mutual development of security together

[800] Because states are woven together in mutual dependence, there is always a danger that security measures in one state can lead to a feeling of insecurity in other states, especially if there is an emphasis on overinsurance

[801] Security policy must therefore continue to be the result of a balance between considerations of both security and restraint combined with the active development of communities of interest

[802] This principle has been further developed in NATO's new strategic concept and through the development of close cooperation between NATO member states and the states that were formerly members of the now dissolved Warsaw Pact

[803] If the concept of collective security is to be realized, international norms of conduct must be expanded, national military autonomy restricted, mutual transparency into states' military dispositions ensured, and collective security and defense arrangements established

[804] The basis for such a process are key international organizations and institutional frameworks that complement each other

[805] UN, CSCE (Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe), NATO, NACC (North Atlantic Cooperation Council), EC and WEU (Western European Union

[806] These have different significance for the design of European security

[807] The development of security communities where common interests appear so strong that it is unthinkable that contradictions will lead to armed conflict exists in the Nordic countries, NATO and the EU

[808] Although the old division of Europe has ended, security policy is still characterized by the existence of nuclear weapons

[809] Nuclear weapons are qualitatively different from other weapons; their role is primarily political

[810] They cannot be "uninvented", and have therefore become part of the political reality that it is up to responsible states to ensure is kept under reassuring control and at the lowest possible level of force

[811] Political goals cannot be realized with the use of nuclear weapons

[812] The nuclear threat helped develop the notion of collective security as an alternative to the notion of national security

[813] The capacity for mutual destruction represents interdependence at its ultimate consequence, and the only possible answer to this challenge is collective security

[814] NATO has played a central role in ensuring that this new understanding gains acceptance

[815] At the same time, the United States' nuclear guarantee in relation to its allies has contributed to stability and acted as a deterrent to war

[816] This still applies, despite the end of the Cold War

[817] Since the country became a NATO member in 1949, Norway's security has been built on full participation in an integrated collective defense system

[818] This has been of crucial importance, partly because there is no military balance of power in the High North

[819] Nor will it do so in the foreseeable future

[820] Through its NATO membership, Norway instead draws on the overall balance of power in the Euro-Atlantic area

[821] It is a fundamental goal of Norwegian security policy to counteract conflicts and any political or military pressure in the North through national efforts, allied cooperation, NATO's collective alliance defense and anchoring in close and binding cooperation with other European democracies

[822] Through Norwegian military efforts and self-defense capabilities, Norway has made it possible for the country's allies to maintain a low military profile in an area that affects particular Russian security interests

[823] This contributes both to stability in the north and thus also to overall stability and peace in Europe

[824] Norway is located in an area that will remain militarily strategically important and sensitive

[825] It is not least the development in the relationship between the United States and Russia that determines how important Norway's military strategic position is at any given time, but also the development in the relationship between Russia and the rest of Europe, especially the European Community, is central

[826] NATO constitutes the most important institutional link linking North America to developments in Europe

[827] NATO's integrated military cooperation and the Atlantic relations are crucial for Norway's security

[828] Integrated military cooperation is built into a close and mutually binding international cooperation system

[829] NATO cooperation has made it possible for Norway to participate actively as a full partner in a peaceful and controllable transformation of post-war Europe

[830] Active American involvement remains vital to ensuring stability and peaceful development in Europe

[831] A NATO in transformation ensures this

[832] NATO also plays a central role as a forum and platform for initiating and implementing measures for arms control and disarmament

[833] The EU's increasing role in European security and the WEU's ambitions to become a link between the EU and NATO, and at the same time constitute the framework for the European pillar of NATO, have changed the conditions for Norway's active participation in shaping the joint Allied positions

[834] Norway's relationship with the development of closer European defense and security cooperation linked to the EC and WEU must be seen in light of the fact that Norway is located in a strategically important and sensitive area, with a need for political and military support

[835] Such an association with North American and European allies remains an important part of Norwegian security policy and must be continuously adapted to changing conditions

[836] Other countries' political and economic decisions are becoming increasingly important for Norway

[837] This is reflected in security policy, where political and economic instruments are gaining greater importance, while the importance of military instruments is changing

[838] National unity important

[839] for security policy Broad national security policy consensus has political intrinsic value, not least for small states in an exposed and vulnerable position

[840] It is therefore a goal in itself to maintain the broad security policy consensus of the post-war period even after the Cold War has ended

[841] The recommendation from the Defence Commission of 1990 shows that this goal has largely been achieved

[842] Subject to the importance attached to the development of the EC, WEU and the European cooperation process in general, and the remaining skepticism towards Norwegian NATO membership, there is a very high level of consensus within the Commission on the description of Norway's security policy framework and the political consequences drawn from this

[843] With the aforementioned reservations, the Defence Commission's work confirms that there is still sufficiently broad national consensus in the area of security policy as a basis for a comprehensive policy, which can achieve broad support both in the Storting and among the Norwegian people

[844] The government aims to build on this agreement, based on the Defense Commission's recommendation

[845] For the details of FK90's security policy analysis and broad political consensus, reference is made to NOU 1992:12, and otherwise to the report's chapter

[846] IMPORTANT INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENTS

[847] The extensive changes in Europe and the former Soviet Union, and the consequences this may have for security in the entire Euro-Atlantic area and for connections between North America and Europe, have changed the political and strategic map in Norway's part of the world

[848] The major change processes will not be completed or stabilized for a long time

[849] Rapid and unexpected developments may occur and the effects will be difficult to predict

[850] In this context, it is all the more important to take a closer look at the key developments that characterize the new era Europe has entered

[851] Norway and the Nordic countries in the new Europe

[852] The security policy pattern in the Nordic region is undergoing transformation and the adjustments in individual country policies are in the process of integrating the Nordic region in a new way into a greatly changed Europe, in which the EC is central

[853] Sweden's and Finland's applications for EC membership signal that the Nordic countries are also moving into a new era

[854] Future membership for the two countries could also entail a form of Swedish and Finnish association with an EC-based security and foreign policy cooperation linked to the WEU

[855] The Swedish and Finnish sides are gradually becoming more open to new forms of cooperation and association in the new Europe, although opinions are divided internally about which forms of association the countries should strive for in relation to expanded defense and security policy cooperation linked to the EC/WEU

[856] The abrogation of the Treaty of Friendship, Security and Cooperation (TSC) between Finland and the former Soviet Union - an agreement that has formed part of the basis of Finnish post-war policy - creates new freedom of action for Finnish foreign policy in the 1990s

[857] The fundamental foreign policy change that has occurred may have implications for the pattern of cooperation in the Arctic, in the Baltic Sea area, and in a broader European context

[858] Against this background, the framework conditions for safeguarding Norwegian security policy have also changed from a Nordic perspective, regardless of Swedish and Finnish EC membership

[859] There is reason to believe that Nordic security will increasingly need to be seen within a broader European framework

[860] During the Cold War, an equilibrium arrangement developed in the Nordic countries, which involved a gradual transition from full integration into the Western defense arrangement for the three westernmost Nordic states of Iceland, Denmark and Norway, through classical Swedish non-alignment to Finland's non-alignment with a SIA pact with the Soviet Union

[861] This balancing arrangement helped to ease the pressure on the individual Nordic countries, thereby promoting restraint on the part of the great powers and stability for the Nordic area

[862] In the new Europe, there will probably be a general need for broader and deeper cooperation in the Nordic region in order to act as a bridge and mediator between a Russia that primarily meets Western Europe in the north, and a Europe that wants to include Russia in a binding cooperation

[863] In order for the Nordic countries to be able to handle this task, so that they are not marginalized in European development and so that they can avoid being drawn into a Russian sphere of influence, Nordic cooperation should be given a clear Western European anchoring

[864] In the area of defense policy, Nordic solutions are not appropriate

[865] Swedish authorities wish to participate actively in the construction of a new European security order in the closest possible connection to the EC

[866] The Swedish EC application does not contain any security policy reservations

[867] The interpretation of Swedish freedom of alliance is compared with the goal of Sweden’s position in a new European security picture

[868] The core of Swedish security policy, however, remains military non-alignment and an independent defense capability, with the aim of remaining neutral in the event of a war in Sweden's immediate vicinity

[869] The changes in Finnish foreign and security policy may seem more far-reaching than those in Sweden

[870] Finland will base its relationship eastward on the new good neighborly agreement with Russia, without military clauses

[871] In contrast to the SIA agreement, this new agreement will not be able to trigger any form of military aid or military cooperation between the two countries

[872] Relations with Western countries are characterized by Finland's openness to new and more binding forms of cooperation with the West

[873] Denmark's position has changed as a result of German unification and 20 years of EC membership

[874] In a military strategic sense, Denmark no longer considers itself part of northern Europe, but as part of NATO's central section

[875] This is reflected in NATO's new command structure, where Denmark has chosen to continue its command-related affiliation with Germany instead of Norway

[876] The Sub-Command for the Baltic Sea Outlets, including the Baltic Sea (BALTAP), nevertheless constitutes a "bridge" between NATO's Central Command and the new Northwest Command, which includes Norway

[877] Denmark seems to place great emphasis on military cooperation with Germany, including through the German-Danish Corps

[878] The new security policy situation in Europe and for the Nordic area has not changed the conditions for Norwegian security policy to the same extent as for Sweden and Finland

[879] The main elements of Norwegian policy are therefore fixed

[880] However, as a result of the end of the Cold War, several adjustments have also been made in Norwegian politics

[881] This applies to certain aspects of the self-imposed restrictions in the north as well as the policy towards Russia as a neighboring state, and affects restrictions on allied aircraft and vessels in Finnmark, call rules and port restrictions, and civil aviation and photography bans, etc

[882] The many disarmament and arms control agreements have introduced a more general multilateral regime that to some extent replaces the political significance of Norway's national self-imposed commitments from the most intense period of the Cold War

[883] In terms of military strategy, neither Norway, Sweden nor Finland - not even together - will have the ability to create a reasonably equal military balance of power with Russia in the north

[884] There is a parallel need to create the necessary security policy support to be able to enter into close cooperation with Russia and to reduce the importance of military factors through political frameworks that link the Nordic area to the EC as the political and economic center of gravity in Europe

[885] Swedish and Finnish reorientation provides opportunities for expanded defense and security cooperation between Nordic countries

[886] Developments have provided an opportunity to lift several of the constraints that attached to cooperation between allied and non-aligned countries in the post-war period

[887] In recent years, an increasingly broader security policy dialogue has developed between the Nordic countries

[888] This happens partly through Nordic cooperation in general and partly through the Nordic defense ministers' meetings and increasing contacts between the individual defense ministries

[889] The work of the Nordic Security Policy Group of Officials has also contributed to the dialogue

[890] The Government aims to actively contribute to further strengthening this dialogue

[891] Russia and the CIS

[892] There is no historical parallel to the disintegration of a nuclear superpower

[893] The attempt to continue some degree of unity through the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) showed that the collapse was total and final

[894] After just one year, CIS appears primarily as a forum for non-binding consultation within a political construct that seems to be becoming increasingly loose

[895] Although the countries affiliated with the CIS may have different intentions regarding the status and role of the Commonwealth, the CIS seems to have become a framework for a controlled dismantling of the old empire

[896] This is reflected in the military area, where the idea of collective security within the framework of the CIS has only been implemented to a very limited extent in practice

[897] The trend seems to be towards major and important states such as Russia and Ukraine establishing their own national defenses, especially in the conventional area

[898] Nuclear weapons, on the other hand, are still formally subject to SUS control

[899] Russia has sought to assume the role of successor to the Soviet Union on the international stage and in terms of control over nuclear weapons

[900] The dispute between Russia and Ukraine over the Black Sea Fleet and the tug-of-war over nuclear weapons have demonstrated that there is an underlying danger of rivalry and conflict between countries affiliated with the CIS

[901] Land-based strategic nuclear weapons are deployed in Russia, Kazakhstan, Ukraine and Belarus

[902] Uncertainty is associated with Ukraine, which on the one hand has declared that all nuclear weapons will be removed from Ukrainian territory, but on the other hand has not signed the Non-Proliferation Treaty

[903] Ukraine has withdrawn from the joint military command of the CIS

[904] Nuclear weapons could play an important role in relations between Russia and Ukraine

[905] Uncertainty has arisen regarding the planned transfer of nuclear weapons from Ukraine to Russia, as Ukraine demands so called administrative control

[906] It is unclear what consequences this could have for Russia's ability to technically secure the weapons

[907] With the exception of Ukraine and Azerbaijan, there also seems to be agreement within the CIS to maintain a common air defense structure

[908] At the Moscow summit in July 1992, it was decided to establish a joint peacekeeping force under the auspices of the CIS for possible deployment to mitigate and stop ethnic conflicts in the territories of the CIS countries

[909] However, the fear that Russia would use such forces as a cover for military intervention in a neighboring state with a Russian minority population has dampened the willingness of the other CIS states to implement the arrangement

[910] Russia, for its part, has already highlighted that the country has vital interests to safeguard along its southern borders, where there is significant conflict potential and where Russian population groups may appear vulnerable, at least from Moscow's perspective

[911] Bilateral defense agreements have been signed between Russia and the Central Asian republics

[912] The Transcaucasian region (Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia) is, in turn, characterized by ethnic, religious and territorial contradictions and disputes

[913] These have already spread into Russian territory, and Moscow has responded with limited use of military force

[914] However, the unrest and disintegration tendencies on Russia's southern flank have the potential to spread further north, into the Russian core area

[915] Russia is in the process of developing a national defense and security policy

[916] However, the process is characterized by the internal power struggle that is ongoing

[917] The starting point for the country's new military doctrine has been presented as "reasonable adequacy

[918] Reductions in Russian military forces and withdrawal from Central and Eastern Europe have already led to significant restructuring problems, which could significantly hamper the implementation of a general restructuring and downsizing of the Russian armed forces

[919] The development of national defenses in the states that are part of the CIS also creates major restructuring problems

[920] million Russians live outside Russia's borders

[921] Developments in Russia's border areas, particularly in the south, and relations with a number of new neighboring states with internal problems will likely consume large parts of Russia's military and emergency preparedness resources

[922] Russia has potentially significant security problems along a number of its borders

[923] Therefore, Russia will have an interest in good, stable and predictable neighborly relations in the north along the borders of the Nordic countries

[924] Russia is facing a long and painful transition, the outcome of which is by no means certain

[925] Developments within this multinational Russia, and the fate of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), represent a significant uncertainty factor for the rest of Europe, not least a neighboring country like Norway

[926] Ethnic and national conflicts

[927] The collapse of the Soviet system revealed a number of historical ethnic, national and religious conflicts in the central and eastern parts of Europe that had been kept in check during the Cold War, but which have remained unresolved

[928] The border demarcations after World War I and World War II and the establishment of new states in the years after World War I created several contradictions and unresolved problems that emerged in full force in the 1990s

[929] This has already led, among other things, to the dissolution - in very different ways - of two of the new state formations of the interwar period: Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia

[930] The legacy of ancient Russia also contributes to this decade's unresolved contradictions, including in the form of various minority groups in Russia and Russian populations in the Baltics, Ukraine, and the Central Asian republics

[931] Next to the Russian minorities outside Russia, the Hungarian minorities in Romania (Transylvania), Slovakia and Serbia (Vojvodina) represent Europe's largest

[932] The rights and status of these minorities can also create contradictions and instability

[933] There are also several signs that indicate that the order that was created in Central and South-Eastern Europe in the years after World War I (the Versailles system) is now in the process of collapsing, both in the Balkans and in the areas around the Carpathians

[934] A significant factor in this context is existing ethnic and national contradictions

[935] The ripple effects of this could be significant for the security policy order in Europe

[936] The dissolution of the Soviet Union not only contributes to new conflict lines from Central Asia to Ukraine

[937] Disputes over borders and ethnicbased conflicts across existing borders, together with major economic and political restructuring problems, also mean that the security policy order in Europe appears very uncertain

[938] Conflict lines and tensions can spread between regions and intensify regional contradictions and disputes

[939] A general demand for "each nation, its own state" could therefore create significant conflict potential in several places in Europe, given the ethnic patchwork that exists; a population pattern that makes it impossible to draw borders that clearly follow ethnic or national dividing lines

[940] The phenomenon of "ethnic cleansing", as expressed in the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, clearly illustrates what can happen when ethnic-national divisions - in this case reinforced through coincident religious and cultural divisions - are made the basis for conflict and abuse against population groups

[941] The war in the former Yugoslavia and the displacement of population groups from their homelands show how cruel conflicts based on ethnic-national antagonisms can be

[942] The ethnic-national conflicts of interest that have today erupted into open conflict in this area may ignite or spill over into other ethnic-national conflicts in other parts of the Balkans

[943] The potential for conflict in Central and Eastern Europe is significant

[944] A number of ethnic and national conflicts in Europe - not just in the Balkans - could lead to regional wars, with the risk of expansion and increased antagonism between surrounding states

[945] This has already prompted the deployment of multinational military forces in peacekeeping and peacebuilding contexts

[946] Expanded and adapted cooperation within a broader European framework can provide the necessary international and multinational guarantees for ethnic minorities and small nations without their own territorial state, so that it will be possible to create stability in Europe and overcome contradictions that could otherwise lead to crises and war

[947] The emergence of a European security and defence identity

[948] While political fragmentation and increased nationalism seem to characterize parts of Central and Eastern Europe, the majority of Western European states have focused on increased integration and supranational cooperation

[949] At the Maastricht summit in December 1991, the EC's heads of state and government decided to establish a European Union that would also include a common foreign and security policy

[950] The Maastricht Treaty, which is partly a revision and partly an expansion of the EC's existing treaty basis, expands foreign and security policy cooperation through the EPS from being limited to the economic and political aspects of security policy to also include defence policy

[951] In this context, the WEU appears as the EU's defense policy tool, which is intended to follow up on joint decisions that have defense policy implications

[952] The common foreign and security policy, including cooperation within the WEU, is based on unanimity between the governments of the participating states

[953] The agreement reached in Maastricht further implies that the WEU will constitute the future basis for a strengthened European pillar in NATO

[954] Whatever the final form

[955] The Maastricht Treaty will have, it must be assumed that the WEU will have a central importance as the European pillar within the alliance

[956] This is in line with the NATO summit in Rome in November 1991 and the decision made there on the development of a European security and defence identity

[957] In the "Rome Declaration" from the meeting, NATO stated that a strengthened role and increased responsibility for the European members of the alliance will contribute to strengthening NATO as a whole as part of the alliance's adaptation to a new Europe

[958] In parallel with the development of a European security and defense role, the crucial trans-Atlantic relations will be further developed

[959] The Atlantic Alliance shall continue to be the main forum for consultations between member states and the meeting place for political decisions related to the security and defence commitments of the Atlantic Pact

[960] The Rome Summit determined that it was up to the countries directly affected to determine concrete measures to develop a common European foreign and security policy, and defense role

[961] Through practical measures, the necessary transparency and complementarity will be ensured between NATO and the European security and defence identity developed through the EC and the WEU

[962] NATO countries welcomed a strengthened role for the WEU, both as a defense component of the European integration process and as a means of strengthening the European pillar of NATO

[963] The EC summit in Maastricht followed up on the framework that the NATO countries had agreed to at the Rome summit

[964] The Maastricht Treaty is also the EU countries' response to the fact that the post-war period has ended, and the need has arisen to find a new basis for a stable European order after the fundamental changes in Europe

[965] The goal is to prevent the European continent from once again being torn apart by ethnic conflicts and national rivalries, with states seeking to secure themselves at the expense of their neighbors

[966] It is of significant importance that, at the same time as the major changes and restructuring taking place in Central and Eastern Europe, stabilizing and security-creating institutions exist and develop in Western Europe, and that these have a broader, common European security perspective

[967] The EC and the WEU appear to be key elements in the new European security order

[968] During the Maastricht meeting in December 1991, the nine WEU countries issued a declaration offering certain EC and NATO countries observer or associate status in the WEU

[969] NATO countries that are not EC members were offered associate WEU membership

[970] This reflected a desire that all European NATO countries should be included in some form of closer European defense cooperation, so that this could constitute a real European pillar within NATO

[971] The Norwegian side has argued that a European pillar in NATO must include all European allies, not just WEU members

[972] When all European NATO countries are given a formalized affiliation to the organization, the WEU will in practice be able to more easily function as the European pillar within NATO

[973] Countries that are associate WEU members will normally have access to participate in all WEU meetings and in all working groups

[974] Associate members will have the right to speak and can help draft unanimity, but will not be able to block consensus

[975] Associate members will not be bound by decisions, but by their own adherence to given decisions, the rights and obligations associated with these decisions will be the same as for member countries

[976] The associate membership does not imply adherence to the modified Brussels Treaty - the basis for the WEU - and is therefore not covered by the WEU's military assistance obligations

[977] Associate members will be asked to contribute financially to the WEU organization

[978] At the ministerial meeting in Rome on 20 November 1992, Norway was admitted as an associate member of the WEU

[979] This association will be effective from the moment Greece ratifies its full WEU membership

[980] In the Government's view, it is crucial to ensure active Norwegian involvement and full participation in the development of the European security and defence identity

[981] Together with NATO membership, Norway's associated membership in the WEU will go a long way towards meeting Norwegian needs, see also section 3.4.3. The Eurogroup, which consists of the defense ministers of the European NATO countries with the exception of France, has been scaled down in line with the development of the WEU

[982] The Eurogroup includes working groups and information activities that will either be transferred to the WEU, NATO or be closed down

[983] The Independent European Programme Group (IEPG) has been decided to be incorporated into the WEU

[984] The IEPG has coordinated European defense equipment production and served as a forum for European defense equipment cooperation

[985] See also sections 4.4.2 and 11.3.6.3. The actual development of WEU cooperation is uncertain, as is the pace and content of the EC process

[986] The question of strengthened military cooperation in the WEU, and thereby also the relationship with NATO's integrated military structure, will probably come up again

[987] The Brussels Treaty, which forms the basis of the WEU, expires in 1998, and the EC countries have planned to hold new intergovernmental conferences to consider possible new treaty changes

[988] Norway must participate in these government conferences in order to contribute actively and safeguard vital Norwegian security interests in a Europe undergoing transformation

[989] It is crucial to ensure that Norway becomes a full part of the new European security and defense identity, which will also form the basis for the European pillar in NATO and for security policy cooperation across the Atlantic

[990] German unification has created challenges in relation to the balance between the Western European powers

[991] Without closer cooperation between larger and smaller states, stability in Europe will not be achieved

[992] Stability in Western Europe appears to be a prerequisite for increased stability in the rest of Europe

[993] Through the EC and WEU, Western countries have institutionalized cooperation that forms a basis for necessary coordination, and which has not least allowed small states to gain influence over joint measures that involve the great powers

[994] There are no security alternatives to continuing binding, mutual cooperation in Europe

[995] A Europe where the great powers once again only sought to safeguard their own interests would not least harm the small states

[996] Norwegian security must remain an integral part of European security

[997] Norway - as a European peripheral nation - must be perceived by the outside world to be of direct security policy interest to the rest of Europe

[998] Norwegian associate membership in the WEU strengthens this objective

[999] The Council of Europe is central to the work for democracy, human rights and social rights, which together express a community of values for the new Europe

[1000] It is the interaction between partially overlapping and interconnected organizations that will shape the new security order in Europe

[1001] Transatlantic relations Security in Europe is closely linked to the continued need for active North American involvement

[1002] Norwegian security is particularly linked to the Atlantic dimension

[1003] NATO holds a key and unique position in Atlantic cooperation

[1004] NATO is the pillar of Norwegian security

[1005] The alliance has provided security and stability in Europe for over 40 years, countering Soviet military power and providing a framework for American engagement in the European security process

[1006] While NATO in the post-war period secured the security interests of Western countries against a centralized Soviet Union with a comprehensive, offensively organized and deployed military capability, NATO faces completely different challenges after the former East/West divide in Europe has disappeared and the Soviet Union has dissolved

[1007] A clear threat has been replaced by unclear and unknown risks and dangers

[1008] NATO countries previously designed their force structure based on a specified mission

[1009] In 1990s Europe, military forces had to adapt to completely different framework conditions and tasks

[1010] NATO countries are in the process of implementing such a transformation, see section

[1011] The Alliance is also making a thorough adaptation to the new Europe and new security challenges, which has consequences for how military forces are used

[1012] A NATO adapted to the new Europe will continue to play a fundamental role in safeguarding Norwegian security

[1013] However, the close ties and cooperation across the Atlantic also take place within a number of other institutional frameworks in addition to NATO

[1014] The United States and Canada are also linked to the Euro-Atlantic security arrangement through their active participation in the CSCE

[1015] In 1990, the US and the EC also signed a bilateral cooperation agreement that involves high-level political consultations several times a year

[1016] Semi-annual meetings between the US President and the President of the European Council and the President of the EC Commission have been established

[1017] Regular meetings also take place between the US Secretary of State and the Presidency of the European Union's Foreign Policy Cooperation

[1018] A similar agreement has been concluded between the EC and Canada

[1019] The CSCE constitutes an important common European framework for cooperation on security issues, but will not alone be able to ensure that the security of the Central and Eastern European states is closely linked to that of Western Europe

[1020] NATO performs a number of key functions and helps ensure the military balance and stability on the European continent

[1021] NATO's fundamental importance is emphasized by the alliance linking North American and European security

[1022] It is significant that NATO now appears to be able to strengthen the CSCE by taking on expanded tasks related to efforts to maintain stability throughout the Euro-Atlantic security area

[1023] Through such reinforcement, peace and stability in Europe can be promoted, and a security vacuum in Eastern Europe can be counteracted

[1024] A continued development of the CSCE, as outlined by the CSCE Summit in Helsinki in the summer of 1992, and the further development of the EC, with the possibility of expansion to more member states, will also contribute to developing and deepening the close cooperation between North American and European states on a broad basis

[1025] It is essential to ensure equal participation from both Russia and other states that have succeeded the Soviet Union in the common European process

[1026] Isolation must be avoided because it promotes instability

[1027] The North Atlantic Cooperation Council (NACC), which originates from NATO, helps to link Russia, other former Soviet states and former Warsaw Pact countries closer to a common European cooperation

[1028] It is also necessary to avoid North America feeling sidelined in relation to the European integration process and the emergence of a new European cooperation structure

[1029] NATO will continue to be the pillar of trans-Atlantic relations and the prerequisite for a continued American military presence in Europe

[1030] The American military presence in Europe will remain crucial, but will also be reduced

[1031] After the fundamental military-strategic and political changes that have occurred since 1989, there is far less reason than before to place decisive emphasis on the overall level of US forces in Europe, as long as it is at a significant level as all American plans envisage

[1032] In any case, Europeans will have to assume a greater share of direct responsibility for their own security in peacetime, and possibly also in the crisis situations that appear most likely

[1033] With the force reductions and reduced defense budgets that can be expected for most European NATO countries, see section 4.4.1, increased European responsibility and efforts will require better coordination and more cooperation in Europe

[1034] This also raises new questions related to the burden sharing between the United States and the European NATO countries, see section 4.4.5. NATO must be continuously transformed and adapted to international developments and the challenges affecting the security interests of the alliance countries

[1035] Key issues such as burden sharing must also be resolved to ensure that NATO is not weakened through reduced support and interest in both the United States and central European countries

[1036] New security policy challenges Security policy challenges for Europe have not only arisen as a result of the major changes within the Euro-Atlantic security area

[1037] Developments outside Europe and North America also represent new challenges, where national borders and geographical distance no longer constitute sufficient or credible protection

[1038] New global factors have gradually emerged as more significant potential conflict factors; these include factors such as energy and raw materials, environmental issues and population explosion, in addition to ethnic, religious and cultural divisions

[1039] European countries face major challenges in relation to development south and east of the Mediterranean

[1040] Much attention is being paid to population explosion, economic and social distress, and the rise of Muslim fundamentalism in neighboring countries to the south

[1041] Developments in North Africa and the Middle East represent serious problems for several European countries, and may help to draw their attention in directions other than Norway's

[1042] In the same way that the northern European member states of the EC contribute to equalization and development in the southern member states, and Western Europe towards Central and Eastern Europe, a comprehensive European policy towards the African and Asian regions to the south and southeast of Europe is considered necessary to promote development and stability

[1043] Secure access to oil and gas supplies is important for Western countries

[1044] Security of energy supplies can affect their foreign and security policy commitments, and their relationship with energy producer Norway, among other things

[1045] Energy and natural resources can be significant as a potential source of conflict

[1046] Control over energy extraction, energy sources and transport could have major international consequences and contribute to exacerbating any crises and conflicts

[1047] Environmental problems and lack of ecological balance can also contribute to insecurity and conflict

[1048] The scarcity of resources could create fertile ground for new problems and pose a potential for conflict, especially in the longer term

[1049] Religiously and culturally based contradictions can trigger conflict

[1050] Europe has been characterized by cultural differences that have partly followed religious dividing lines

[1051] Religious and cultural dividing lines still run through Europe, not least in the Balkans, but also in other parts of both Eastern and Western Europe

[1052] In general, they often coincide with ethnic dividing lines, and act mutually reinforcingly

[1053] In North Africa and the Middle East, there are several states that are on the threshold of acquiring nuclear weapons

[1054] The technological proliferation of the ability to produce weapons of mass destruction (WMD), together with long-range delivery means in the form of ballistic missiles, represents a new security policy challenge for Europe

[1055] The combination of such technology, along with social and economic unrest and distress, and religious and ethnic antagonisms, can amplify such a new challenge

[1056] What all new challenges have in common is that they are difficult to solve if states act on their own

[1057] They must therefore be solved jointly

[1058] Economic strength and high technology

[1059] as an international power factor Military power still constitutes a significant power factor in international politics

[1060] However, international economic power is emerging as increasingly important

[1061] The key to international influence has, over the past few decades, been based more strongly than previously on economic strength and economic relations with other countries

[1062] This is particularly true where economic dependence is unbalanced, with dependence and vulnerability of dependent states as a prominent feature

[1063] Economic development is characterized by internationalization and globalization

[1064] Previously purely national businesses and multinational corporations are establishing themselves in an increasing number of countries, and trade and capital flows have political impacts that often also include security policy aspects

[1065] Dependence on certain raw materials or finished goods can pose a potential or explicit security risk and can create fertile ground for conflicts of interest between states

[1066] Competition for market share and competition-distorting national support schemes can also lead to conflicts of interest or rivalry, even between countries that are closely linked through extensive cooperation

[1067] Negotiations on customs and tariff provisions, including under the auspices of GATT, can reduce the likelihood of this happening, but can also exacerbate the problems if they do not lead to progress

[1068] High technology and specialized knowledge have become an increasingly important part of international economic competition

[1069] In part, the technology factor follows trade and investment flows, in part it represents a separate "category of goods" suitable for buying and selling

[1070] Much of the high technology has military applications in addition to civilian ones, but some technology is primarily considered military

[1071] Both high-tech weapons and other advanced equipment with military applications and trade in high-tech military technology represent a potential or real security risk

[1072] Such trade seems difficult to control, and the unwanted spread of military high technology could have unpredictable consequences

[1073] A main problem, however, is that much high technology can have both military and civilian applications

[1074] It is the user who ultimately decides which application

[1075] such technology should be obtained, despite the fact that there may be express agreements that it should only be used for civilian activities

[1076] Over the past couple of decades, the international economy has developed towards a certain regionalization, with a focus on dominant national economies and currencies

[1077] Three such "centers" stand out

[1078] the "yen zone" with Japan as the center, the "dollar zone" with the United States as the center and the "mark zone" with Germany as the center

[1079] As a result of the EC process, the latter is nevertheless to be considered an "ECU zone" with the EC as the center

[1080] The latter will become more prominent once the EC internal market has been established, and will become the dominant feature if the Maastricht Treaty's premise of establishing an economic and monetary union becomes a reality towards the end of the 1990s

[1081] The economic competition between these three centers may increasingly have security policy consequences if conflicts of interest and open rivalry are allowed to dominate at the expense of common interests

[1082] Not least, trade policy disputes and economic contradictions across the Atlantic can have effects both on Western European - and thus in turn common European - cooperation, and on NATO and transatlantic cooperation more generally, if such contradictions are not handled sensibly

[1083] The danger of this type of contradiction is present and may increase in times of economic downturn

[1084] Economic conflicts of interest already play a more important role in security policy, affecting the possibility of finding common solutions and establishing security together

[1085] Economic power can give a state foreign policy room for manoeuvre, but also has its clear limitations

[1086] The impact is greatest when economic power is simultaneously combined with other international power factors, particularly political / diplomatic power and military power

[1087] This is, among other things, what has been the basis for the United States' status as a superpower, with the enormous international influence the country has had after World War II

[1088] In recent years, however, the United States' foreign policy space has been reduced relatively, due to the emergence of new economic and technological centers on the world stage, because the relevance of military power - at least in the context of a major conflict - has diminished after the end of the Cold War, and because the United States' own foreign economic freedom of action has been greatly reduced as a result of large trade and payments deficits and a rapidly increasing national debt

[1089] The German economy, in turn, has contributed to giving German authorities increased freedom of action in relations with the countries of Eastern Europe, not least Russia

[1090] The German economy was also a prerequisite for German unification to be carried out so quickly

[1091] After the Soviet collapse, the German economy, even with the large resources used to rebuild and modernize Eastern Germany, emerged as an economic and thus political connection point for the Central and Eastern European countries

[1092] Germany provides by far the largest economic assistance to the East, especially to the Soviet Union, later Russia

[1093] Germany is also paying for the withdrawal of Russian troops from German territory

[1094] However, the enormous need for support and assistance for the former Eastern Bloc shows that no single country is capable of playing a decisive role alone

[1095] The European Commission has played a central role in coordinating the overall economic and logistical support from West to East since the end of the Cold War

[1096] The same applies to the EC countries' aid programs towards North Africa and the Third World more generally

[1097] NATO'S ROLE

[1098] IN THE NEW EUROPE NATO's new strategic concept was adopted by the heads of state and government at the Rome Summit in November 1991 and forms the basis for the Alliance's security policy in the new Europe, including a principled and guiding description of the role of the armed forces in peace, crisis and war

[1099] Through the follow-up Oslo Decision of June 1992, NATO is prepared to support peacekeeping efforts under the auspices of the CSCE or the UN, by making the Alliance's available resources and expertise available for peacekeeping operations

[1100] This decision is a follow-up to the strategic concept's emphasis on crisis prevention and crisis management

[1101] The Strategic Concept is an agreed document that describes the strategic context, the Alliance's objectives and security policy functions, its broad approach to the concept of security and the guidelines for Alliance defense

[1102] The document forms the basis for NATO's new force structure, command structure, reinforcement plans, force objectives, and thereby for the alliance defense of which the Norwegian Armed Forces will be a part in the years to come

[1103] For this reason, the concept also governs Norwegian defense policy and the requirements and tasks that are important for the future Norwegian defense structure

[1104] The principles, tasks and characteristics that are the basis for NATO's new strategic concept will govern NATO's collective defense in the 1990s and thereby constitute a crucial framework factor for Norwegian security

[1105] The main points of the strategic concept are presented in the following subchapters

[1106] The Alliance's objectives and security policy functions

[1107] The underlying element of NATO's security policy, with the preservation of peace as its goal, will continue to be the maintenance of a military capability sufficient to prevent war and, if necessary, ensure effective defence

[1108] The starting point is that no NATO country should be forced to rely solely on its national resources if the country is faced with a security policy challenge

[1109] This is a contribution to stability in Europe

[1110] The Alliance's armed forces are intended to represent a means of dealing with crises that affect the security of member countries

[1111] The Alliance has four core functions according to the Strategic Concept: Forming the basis for a stable security policy environment in Europe

[1112] No country should be able to threaten any European country, or impose its will on it by the threat or use of force

[1113] Serve as a trans-Atlantic forum for Allied consultations on any issue affecting the vital interests of member states

[1114] Deter and defend against any threat of attack against the territory of any NATO member country, and 4) preserve the strategic balance in Europe

[1115] The Strategic Concept states that other European institutions such as the EC, WEU and CSCE also have roles to play in fulfilling these core functions, in accordance with their respective responsibilities and purposes

[1116] NATO's broad membership and instruments put the alliance in a special position in that it is able to carry out all core functions

[1117] A broad security policy approach

[1118] The Alliance has always sought to achieve its objectives of safeguarding the security and territorial integrity of its member states and establishing a just and lasting peace in Europe using both political and military means

[1119] This is still valid

[1120] With the new security policy situation in Europe, the possibilities for achieving these goals using various political instruments are greater than before

[1121] NATO's ability to handle the many and new security policy challenges requires a broad approach to the concept of security

[1122] This is reflected in the alliance's security policy strategy, where dialogue, cooperation and maintaining the capability for collective defense reinforce and support each other

[1123] These three elements aim to reduce the risk of conflict as a result of misunderstanding or calculated risk, to build increased mutual understanding and trust between all European countries, to contribute to successful crisis management in the event of crises affecting the security of the Member States, and to increase the possibilities for creating a real partnership between all European countries based on common security problems

[1124] The strategic concept provides a broad description of the practical implementation of the three main security policy elements: dialogue, cooperation and collective defense

[1125] This forms the main basis for NATO's security policy in the new Europe. The Alliance's arms control and disarmament policy contributes to both dialogue and cooperation with other states, and will continue to play an important role in NATO's ability to achieve its security policy objectives

[1126] The purpose is to promote security and stability at the lowest possible force level and in accordance with purely defense requirements

[1127] NATO will continue to respect the legitimate security interests of other states and seek to resolve conflicts peacefully in accordance with the UN Charter

[1128] The Alliance will work for peaceful and friendly international relations and support democratic institutions

[1129] Guidelines for military defence The NATO summit in London in the summer of 1990 established the central guidelines for the alliance's future military strategy and force structure

[1130] The strategic concept gives these guidelines a unified and holistic form, and is based on a mix of continuity and innovation

[1131] The following principles continue to underpin the alliance's strategy

[1132] NATO's armed forces have as their most important task the task of ensuring the territorial integrity and sovereignty of its member states

[1133] None of NATO's weapons will ever be used for anything other than self-defense

[1134] NATO has no defined adversary

[1135] The Allies will maintain sufficient military strength to convince a potential aggressor that the use of force directed against the territory of member countries will be met with collective and effective measures by all of them, and that the risks of such aggression will outweigh the perceived gains

[1136] The Alliance's military forces must therefore be able to defend the Alliance's borders, stop an aggressor's advance as far forward as possible, and maintain or restore the territorial integrity of any member state

[1137] The goal is to end the war quickly by making the attacker reconsider his decision, halt the attack, and retreat

[1138] The security of the Allies is indivisible

[1139] an attack on one is an attack on all

[1140] Alliance solidarity and strategic unity are therefore crucial prerequisites for collective security

[1141] The achievement of NATO's goals is entirely dependent on both a fair division of roles, risks and responsibilities, and on the sharing of the benefits of collective defence

[1142] The presence of North American conventional and US nuclear forces in Europe remains crucial, linking European security to North American security

[1143] The collective aspects of alliance defense are embodied in practical measures that enable Allies to gain decisive political, military and resource advantages in the form of collective defense

[1144] This prevents a renationalization of defense policy, but does not deprive the member states of sovereignty

[1145] The practical implementation is based both on an integrated military structure and on cooperation and coordination agreements

[1146] Key elements are collective force planning, joint operational planning, multinational forces, stationing of forces outside one's own territory - on a reciprocal basis where appropriate, measures for crisis management and reinforcements, consultation procedures, common standards and procedures for equipment, training and logistics, joint and combined military exercises, and cooperation on infrastructure, materiel procurement and logistics

[1147] To protect peace and prevent war or any form of coercion, NATO will maintain an appropriate mix of nuclear and conventional forces deployed in Europe and in good standing for the foreseeable future, but at a clearly reduced level

[1148] Both elements are crucial to the security of the alliance, and they cannot replace each other

[1149] The new security policy environment nevertheless makes it possible for NATO to implement drastic changes in the military area

[1150] The deployment of forces will be far less advanced than before, the standing forces will be fewer and generally have a lower level of readiness, and the principle of flexible response will be changed to reflect a reduced reliance on nuclear weapons

[1151] The armed forces in peace, crisis and war

[1152] The fundamental purpose of the armed forces to guarantee the security and territorial integrity of the Member States remains

[1153] The Alliance's new strategic concept nevertheless reflects the necessity of taking into account that in the new political, military and strategic environment, the previously unambiguous, massive and comprehensive threat has given way to diverse and multidimensional challenges

[1154] According to this strategic concept, NATO's armed forces have different tasks in peace, crisis and war

[1155] In peacetime, they should be able to safeguard the security of the Member States against any risks that may exist, contribute to maintaining stability and balance in Europe and ensure that peace is maintained, also in close cooperation with other international organisations

[1156] NATO's armed forces can contribute to dialogue and cooperation throughout Europe by participating in both confidence-building measures and in the verification of arms control agreements

[1157] NATO's armed forces must also be able to provide the necessary assurance against potential challenges, at the minimum level necessary to prevent war

[1158] In the event of crises that could lead to a military threat to the security of member states, NATO's armed forces must be able to contribute to successful crisis management and to a peaceful solution

[1159] This requires that the forces have the ability to respond appropriately at the right time, the ability to deter hostile actions, and the ability to repel aggression

[1160] NATO's military forces must therefore also be adapted to the demands posed by the possibility of a major conflict, even though the probability of a major conflict is currently small

[1161] The strategic concept also describes in detail how NATO's conventional forces must be built up to be able to carry out their assigned tasks

[1162] NATO's land, sea and air forces will need to cooperate closely and have the ability to conduct combined operations

[1163] Land forces are crucial to the ability to hold or regain territory

[1164] Most of them will normally have a relatively low level of preparedness and will rely to a greater extent than before on mobilization and reserves

[1165] The naval forces, with their mobility, flexibility and endurance, will be an important part of NATO's ability to handle crises

[1166] Their main tasks are to ensure sea control to secure the Alliance's maritime lines of communication, to support land and amphibious operations, and to protect NATO's sea-based nuclear deterrent forces

[1167] The air forces can operate both separately and in combined operations

[1168] The tasks include interception, offensive air support, surveillance and electronic warfare

[1169] Air forces are crucial to the overall effectiveness of NATO's armed forces

[1170] Their function in relation to support operations both over land and at sea requires the ability to deploy over long distances and refuel in the air

[1171] Air defense forces, including modern command and control systems for air operations, are necessary to ensure air superiority

[1172] For a more detailed discussion of the requirements that political and military-technological developments place on military forces that are to be able to operate effectively in the 1990s, see sections 4.5 and 4.6. In order to be able to provide flexible responses to different challenges, the strategic concept requires effective surveillance and intelligence, flexible command and control arrangements, mobility between NATO's various command sections, effective supply arrangements and sufficient transport capacity

[1173] The Alliance's ability to build up larger, well-equipped and trained forces at a sufficient level when needed is fundamental to both crisis management and defense

[1174] This includes the ability to reinforce any area of the member states' territories that may be exposed to a threat and to establish a multinational military presence if and when required

[1175] Both transfers of forces within Europe and across the Atlantic require control of the necessary lines of communication as well as support and exercises

[1176] Civilian resources will become increasingly important in this context

[1177] Collective measures will increasingly be based on multinational forces that will complement national contributions to NATO

[1178] The multinational emergency response forces make it possible, among other things, to deploy forces with more flexible combat capabilities than can be made available by individual member states alone, thereby contributing to a more efficient use of scarce resources

[1179] The fundamental purpose behind the Allies' nuclear forces is political: to preserve peace and prevent any form of coercion and war

[1180] Nuclear weapons will continue to play a crucial war-preventing role by guaranteeing that any potential aggressor will feel uncertain about how NATO will be able to respond to military aggression

[1181] They make it clear that aggression, whatever it may be, is not a rational path to take

[1182] The ultimate guarantee of the security of the Allies lies in strategic nuclear weapons, especially American ones

[1183] The independent nuclear forces of the United Kingdom and France, which have their own deterrent roles, contribute to overall deterrence and to the security of the alliance

[1184] A credible nuclear force structure and unequivocal Allied solidarity and shared commitment to preventing war, according to the Strategic Concept, require continued broad participation by Allied countries participating in collective defence in terms of nuclear roles, the stationing of nuclear weapons on their territory in peacetime, and arrangements for command, control and consultation

[1185] NATO will retain some nuclear weapons in Europe at the minimum level necessary to preserve peace and stability, limited to air-delivered weapons, and if necessary, supplemented by sea-based systems

[1186] According to the Unified Strategic Concept, the Alliance's remaining nuclear weapons will represent weapons of last resort

[1187] Sub-strategic weapons will not normally be deployed on surface vessels and attack submarines

[1188] There is no need for nuclear artillery or ground-based, short-range nuclear missiles

[1189] See also section

[1190] The strategic concept will also guide NATO's policy regarding nuclear weapons

[1191] NATO's active adaptation

[1192] The foundation for NATO's active adaptation to the new Europe was laid at the London Summit in the summer of

[1193] After the Strategic Concept was finally adopted in November 1991, NATO defense ministers adopted three new military management documents

[1194] a supplementary and subordinate military strategy document on the implementation of the strategic concept in the military area, the principles for NATO's new force structure and a new reinforcement concept

[1195] Important decisions were also made regarding NATO's new command structure

[1196] The latter was followed up with more detailed decisions

[1197] NATO's new force structure is described in Parliamentary Resolution No

[1198] The main points are fewer standing forces, especially in Central Europe, reduced readiness for most of them, more withdrawn deployment, increased emphasis on multinationality, increased flexibility and mobility, and the ability to rebuild larger forces if needed

[1199] NATO operates with three main categories of forces

[1200] Main defense forces whose primary task is to defend a given area

[1201] These can be standing or mobilization forces

[1202] Norwegian military forces will primarily be main defense forces

[1203] Emergency response forces which are multinational forces with high readiness and great mobility

[1204] These will become NATO's most important military tool for crisis management

[1205] The emergency forces are divided into two categories

[1206] Immediate Reaction Forces (IRF) and significantly larger Rapid Reaction Forces (RRF

[1207] Both will consist of forces from all three branches of the armed forces

[1208] The IRF will be based on an expansion of NATO's so-called "fire brigade" (ACE Mobile Forces AMF), which consists of both an air and land component

[1209] The land military part of the RRF will consist of a multinational corps that will consist of, among other things, several multinational divisions (ACE Rapid Reaction Corps - ARRC

[1210] A number of NATO member states have also made aircraft units available to the RRF

[1211] On the naval side, a multinational standing force (Standing Naval Force SNF) will be established, building on the standing naval units that NATO currently has in the Atlantic (STANAVFORLANT), the English Channel (STANAVFORCHAN) and the Mediterranean (STANAVFORMED), respectively

[1212] Such a standing force can be assembled as needed and according to any missions that may arise

[1213] Allied air and naval forces will be of great importance for the ability to quickly reinforce the defense of Norway

[1214] In line with the recommendation from the majority of the Defence Commission, the Government, after consulting the Storting, has decided that Norway will participate in the IRF with all three branches of defence (see section

[1215] Active and full Norwegian participation in the IRF will be the most important instrument that links Norway directly to NATO's collective defense and to the emergency response forces as a military tool for crisis management and war prevention (see section

[1216] Additional forces that will primarily consist of US standing forces and reserve forces stationed in the United States

[1217] These will require longer notice periods before they can be deployed in Europe and will also be dependent on extensive transport capacity

[1218] The European national forces that are not included in the other two main categories will also be considered additional forces

[1219] NATO's new force structure is expected to be completed by 1995, while new reinforcement plans to implement the new reinforcement concept are expected to be ready by mid

[1220] An important point is that forces from all three main categories are expected to be included in the reinforcement plans

[1221] Allied reinforcements within Europe should be able to take place both within a given command section (e.g. the Northwest Region) and between two command sections (e.g. from the Central Region to the Northwest Region

[1222] The implementation of NATO's new force structure in the conventional area is closely linked to the implementation of the CFE Agreement, including CFE-1A on personnel strength increases, by the end of

[1223] When it comes to nuclear weapons, the adaptation to a new force structure has essentially already been completed

[1224] The withdrawal of short-range land- and sea-based US nuclear weapons from Europe was completed during the first half of 1992 (including cruise missiles and nuclear weapons for land-based naval aircraft

[1225] Compared to the 1980s, NATO's nuclear weapons in Europe have been reduced by approximately 80 percent

[1226] There will only be 6-8000 sub-strategic nuclear weapons left (free-falling aircraft-based bombs) of the approximately 4,000 sub-strategic nuclear weapons of various types that NATO previously had in Europe

[1227] NATO countries will continue to emphasize the political role and war-deterrent function of nuclear weapons

[1228] This does not entail any changes to Norway's established nuclear weapons policy

[1229] NATO's new command structure is described in detail and is leaner than before, especially in Central Europe

[1230] Norway is part of the new Northwest Command together with the United Kingdom, the Baltic Sea, the North Sea and the English Channel

[1231] Norwegian forces are thus part of a joint command with British forces and naval forces from Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Belgium

[1232] The new command structure is scheduled to be fully implemented by the end of

[1233] The practical implementation of the decisions that have been made will be crucial for how NATO's collective defense will be and function

[1234] This primarily applies to the force structure and command structure, as well as the other common elements assumed in the strategic concept

[1235] Important new international events may change the assumptions and require a reassessment of some of the key decisions that have been made

[1236] The practical follow-up to NATO's goal of dialogue and cooperation led as early as December 1991 to the establishment of the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (NACC), which currently numbers 37 states (the 16 NATO countries, 21 countries from the Warsaw Pact and the dissolved Soviet Union, in addition to Albania
