[1237] Through a separate military cooperation group (Group on Defence Matters GDM), an action program has been prepared for increased contact, dialogue and practical cooperation

[1238] NATO's Military Committee actively participates in this cooperation, as do NATO's other military bodies

[1239] The decision to support peacekeeping operations under the auspices of and mandated by the CSCE or the UN illustrates the Alliance's new focus on crisis management

[1240] As political procedures, military plans, armed forces with support structures, etc., come into place, NATO will be prepared to play a more prominent role in the event that new crises and problems arise in Europe or adjacent areas

[1241] NATO will continue to constitute a credible framework for the collective defense on which Norway's security is based

[1242] However, it will be a significantly reshaped NATO, where the emergence of a European security and defense identity will have increasing consequences for how NATO will function and adapt further

[1243] The WEU will gain greater importance, also for NATO cooperation

[1244] An increasing part of the ongoing trans-Atlantic dialogue will take place between the US and the EC

[1245] SECURITY POLICY CHALLENGES

[1246] After the extensive changes since 1989, not least the dissolution of the Soviet Union and the establishment of the Russian Federation, there is no immediate military threat to Norway

[1247] Nevertheless, Norway must still take into account the extensive military forces stationed on the Kola Peninsula and in northwestern Russia

[1248] The development of the Russian forces in the north is described in more detail under section

[1249] The term "threat" encompasses an expressed or potential intent

[1250] It is the possible use of armed force by a state or political regime that is at the core of the concept of threat, not the weapons themselves

[1251] If it can be written off as unthinkable that a neighboring country would threaten or use armed force, i.e. when a real security community has been created, it is of no security policy significance to consider the neighboring country's military forces as a potential threat, or to be concerned with one's own defense capabilities in relation to this country

[1252] From the Norwegian side, for example, we are not concerned with the defense capability against Sweden or the offensive military capacity inherent in the Swedish Air Force

[1253] Norway's relationship with a Russia undergoing rapid change must also be viewed in this light

[1254] However, there has not yet been a normalization and stabilization of political conditions in Russia that could justify a conclusion that this great power's significant military forces are to be considered of no significance to Norway's security

[1255] On the contrary, there is still great uncertainty and unpredictability related to developments in Russia and the country's political, economic and social reform process

[1256] If there is to be a military threat, it must, in addition to encompassing an offensive military capability and geographical reach, also encompass an expressed or potential political intent and offensive military operations as possible means of achieving a set political goal

[1257] The future political order in Russia is very uncertain

[1258] This poses a structural uncertainty that Norway and the rest of Europe must deal with

[1259] Politically and analytically, however, it is crucial to base a realistic assessment of Norway's future security policy position towards Russia on nuanced assumptions

[1260] It is particularly important to recognize that the assumptions that applied during the Cold War are no longer valid

[1261] Norwegian security policy must help Norway safeguard its vital interests and meet new and changing conditions and challenges

[1262] The concept of "security policy challenge" is far broader than the concept of threat that was previously strongly focused on

[1263] Such a challenge means that emphasis is placed on international changes and development trends, the general policies of other states, individual decisions or actions, etc. that could have negative consequences for Norway's security and vital Norwegian interests

[1264] Russia as a security policy challenge

[1265] The most serious security policy challenge that Norway faces in its relationship with Russia is related to the significant military capacity that Russia has in the north or can transfer there

[1266] Russia's offensive military force is far greater than what Norway can balance or defend itself against alone in the event of armed aggression

[1267] A credible Norwegian military defense capability against this eventuality will necessarily have to be based on allied military reinforcements, of a scale that, together with Norwegian military forces, would be sufficient to repel the attack and restore Norway's territorial integrity

[1268] Norway's position in a strategic perspective, challenges and potential threats, in addition to Russia's military capacity in the High North, are described in more detail in chapters 4.1 and

[1269] If Norway were to stand isolated and alone without a credible military defense and collective security guarantees behind it, rivalry between Russia and other great powers could also lead to situations where an isolated and limited military attack against Norway could move closer

[1270] This underlines the continued importance of the political and military backing that NATO provides

[1271] Collective military security guarantees will remain crucial to prevent pressure and threats in unforeseen situations

[1272] It is impossible to estimate how likely it is that political changes in Russia will lead to long-term contradictions and rivalry between Russia and the rest of Europe, including Norway, NATO and the United States

[1273] However, Norwegian security policy cannot ignore this type of eventuality

[1274] The most likely consequence of a nationalist and authoritarian regime in Moscow would probably come in the form of tension and crises in relations with a number of former Soviet republics along Russia's western and southern borders

[1275] In such a situation, it could be in Russia's interest to maintain stable conditions and relatively low tension in the northwest in order to free up military resources and avoid the risk of conflict along too many borders simultaneously

[1276] However, the Kola Peninsula's great strategic importance to Russia is unlikely to allow military depletion

[1277] Another important point, with significant consequences for Norway's security policy position in the new Europe, is that Russia's military forces and offensive potential in the north are no longer linked to an extensive advanced and offensively organized military apparatus in Central Europe

[1278] In a possible acute crisis in relations between Norway and Russia in the north, with a need for allied military transfers to establish a local military balance of power and prevent the use of military force from appearing as an acceptable solution and an alternative course of action that could yield gains from the Russian perspective, Norway's allies on the continent will therefore have a different military freedom of action than they had in the post-war period

[1279] Should military operations occur in the north, this could initially take the form of a regional conflict

[1280] These are the kinds of potential challenges that NATO's new strategic concept primarily aims to address, in the form of various measures for crisis management, regional force building and, if necessary, an adequate capability for collective defense

[1281] Even though a major conflict today appears unlikely, it cannot be ruled out, and must therefore also be included in the basis for the development of Norwegian defense in the 1990s

[1282] In the future disarmament process, Norway should strive to reduce Russian offensive capacity in the High North

[1283] This can happen through restructuring and establishing regional initiatives within a broader international framework

[1284] It is a fundamental goal for Norway to link strong societal interests in Russia to peaceful cooperation with the country's Nordic neighbors

[1285] The Norwegian proposal for close multilateral cooperation in the Barents Region, and the new Baltic Sea Council established in 1992, are important elements in such a political strategy

[1286] Russia has significant potential for petroleum production, especially natural gas from the Barents Sea region

[1287] Development of offshore deposits and the construction of a gas transportation system could provide a good basis for developing economic cooperation in the region

[1288] It would also reduce both Russia's and Western Europe's vulnerability to unstable conditions in the areas that are currently the main sources, particularly for natural gas

[1289] Because the relationship between a great power and a small neighboring state will always entail potential problems for the small state, it is crucial to link Norway's relationship with Russia to a larger and multilateral political framework

[1290] Norway must not risk that Russia may pursue one type of policy towards continental Europe, based on Russian needs, and another policy towards Norway in the north, based on Russian demands

[1291] In order to have political freedom of action and the necessary backing to enter into close and comprehensive cooperation with Russia, Norway will therefore need to be an integrated part of a larger Western community

[1292] Russia depends on a good relationship with the EC for its economic and political development

[1293] It is important for Norway not to be seen as a small Northern European peripheral state, but as part of the political and economic mainstream in Europe

[1294] Norwegian membership in the European Community will help to underpin and ensure an equal partnership in the North, by safeguarding the political and economic security policy aspects of the relationship with Russia

[1295] NATO membership, in turn, provides Norway with the military security guarantees that are still required

[1296] Depending on the outcome of the internal power struggle in Russia and the implementation of the arms control agreements that have been concluded, the purely military factors in Russia's relations with Western countries will take a back seat

[1297] This will also have beneficial effects for Norway and further reduce the likelihood of a military conflict in the north

[1298] The Cold War had its origins in Central Europe and the divided Germany

[1299] At that time, it was desirable and right to shield the relatively low tension in the north and Norway's relationship with the Soviet Union from the high tension associated with, among other things, Berlin's status

[1300] In the new Europe, however, the situation is the opposite of what it was in the post-war period

[1301] It is therefore now desirable and right for Norway to link its relationship with Russia in the north as closely as possible to Russia's relationship with the EC and continental Europe in order to ensure a good and equal cooperative relationship between Norway and Russia

[1302] Norway must also connect to the stabilizing low-tension area in Europe to avoid the development of new voltage conditions in the highlands

[1303] Developments in Europe as a security policy challenge

[1304] As a result of international interdependence and Norway's close political, economic and cultural ties with the rest of Europe, crises and conflicts in parts of Europe other than the Nordic countries could also have serious security policy consequences for Norway

[1305] In contrast to Norway's relationship with Russia, such consequences will mainly be of an indirect nature

[1306] They will nevertheless be able to have a negative impact on important Norwegian interests

[1307] In the economic area, Norway's relations with the rest of Europe are of vital importance, and instability and crises that weaken economic development in Europe will easily have direct negative economic and social effects in Norway

[1308] If political fragmentation and a relapse into national rivalry were to become a general European phenomenon after the end of the Cold War and the ideologically based European division has been overcome, there would be a real danger that the entire European edifice based on common norms of behavior, mutually binding cooperation and attempts to establish a new security community could collapse

[1309] The result would be an unstable and insecure Europe characterized by the same serious problems that characterized the period between the two world wars

[1310] For Norway, the security policy implications of such a development would not least come as a result of the consequences it would have for political developments in Russia and Russia's relations with its surroundings

[1311] In the Government's view, it is crucial that collective security and defense arrangements can be established that bridge the old East/West divide and prevent the emergence of new dividing lines

[1312] Here, the UN, CSCE, NATO, the EC and the WEU complement each other

[1313] When it comes to the economic and political aspects of security in Europe, the EC process is at the center

[1314] It is a key security policy goal for Norway to actively contribute to the work of creating a stable and predictable European order based on the principle of collective security

[1315] Without binding international cooperation through the organizations that are most central to European development, this principle cannot be realized

[1316] Active responsibility for European development means that Norway must also be prepared and able to participate in multinational operations

[1317] The Government aims for active Norwegian participation in international institutions and organizations that are important for Norway's security in order to ensure co-determination and safeguard the need for Norwegian influence on decisions and processes that can have both direct and indirect consequences for Norwegian security

[1318] Only active participation gives small states the necessary co-determination

[1319] A crucial security policy challenge for Norway in the new Europe is to reach a position that makes the country an active and full participant in the crucial decision-making forums

[1320] If small states are to have the opportunity to exercise influence and co-determination in the major issues that the great powers have traditionally handled on their own, often in competition with each other, binding international cooperation is required through institutions that ensure their right to equal participation

[1321] Active Norwegian participation in favor of European security and stability in other parts of Europe will increasingly appear as a prerequisite for the rest of Europe to perceive developments in northern Europe and Norway's relationship with Russia as a common European concern

[1322] Norway's application for membership in the EC must also be seen in this light

[1323] The development of a European security and defence identity and of transatlantic relations as a security policy challenge Through the development of the European security and defence identity, the European and Atlantic processes intersect

[1324] Militarily, NATO and active American participation in ensuring European security and stability will continue to be crucial for Norwegian security

[1325] In order to meet American expectations and contribute to Europeans assuming a greater share of direct responsibility for their own security in peacetime, and possibly also in the crisis situations that appear most likely, it is a key security policy challenge for Norway to actively participate in shaping the European security and defense identity that cooperation in both the WEU and the continued implementation of the adaptation work in NATO presupposes

[1326] Norway's associate membership in the WEU is an important tool here

[1327] The Government considers it essential to contribute to the development of European cooperation in the area of defence policy in a way that takes into account transatlantic political and military needs

[1328] This also requires the opportunity for active participation in all relevant decision-making bodies

[1329] Together with NATO membership, Norway's associate membership in the WEU will go a long way towards meeting Norwegian security needs in this context

[1330] However, Norway will only be able to participate fully in the development of the new security policy order in Europe through EC membership

[1331] Other security policy challenges

[1332] The danger of the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction (WMD), together with long-range delivery means in the form of ballistic missiles, represents a new security policy challenge for Europe to which Norway cannot remain passive

[1333] Despite the fact that Norway is geographically quite sheltered, the indirect consequences of this development could affect vital Norwegian interests

[1334] Norway may also be affected by new challenges related to population development in the south and southeast of Europe

[1335] Also when it comes to the possibility of formulating political solutions to such problems, it is crucial that Norway can participate in the political decision-making forums that have the necessary power of action and sufficient diplomatic and economic resources

[1336] When it comes to terrorism and acts of violence in Europe stemming from conflicts in the Third World, particularly the Middle East, Norway has no guarantee that Norwegian interests will not also become a relevant target

[1337] Effective countermeasures in this field, in the same way as measures against the smuggling and sale of drugs, which are increasingly perceived as a threat to Western societies, are a common challenge that must therefore be solved jointly

[1338] NORWAY'S SECURITY POLICY GOALS

[1339] St. report no. 54 (1987-88) discussed the fundamental goals of Norwegian security policy, with reference to St. report no. 74 (1982-83) and Recommendation S no

[1340] The Storting passed the Recommendation

[1341] S no. 160 (1988-89) agreed that these goals were fixed and had been given the same formulation in the Storting report on the main guidelines for the Armed Forces' activities in the period 1989-93 as in the previous long-term report for the period

[1342] Given the stable framework conditions that prevailed during the Cold War, it was natural that the formulation of Norway's security policy goals was also fixed

[1343] FKO's review of new security policy developments formed the basis for the recommendations made by the majority of the Commission regarding Norway's position in the international security and defense landscape

[1344] The Commission's recommendation was prepared during a period characterized by major international upheavals

[1345] The transition to a new era in European security makes it relevant to consider the fundamental goals of Norwegian security policy

[1346] The new security policy situation and the various, multifaceted and partly new security policy challenges that this entails for Norway and European security, make it necessary to assess the instruments and the relative weight given to them

[1347] This is closely linked to the follow-up of security policy goals

[1348] A main conclusion in NATO's strategic concept is that the political aspects of security policy have gained increased relative importance at the expense of the military aspects

[1349] Another important reformulation in this allied management instrument is related to the role of the armed forces in peace, crisis and war, see section

[1350] The Armed Forces will be able to have an expanded role in peacetime

[1351] The transition from peace to conflict may become more fluid than before

[1352] This could affect when and how military forces are used

[1353] It is important that the Norwegian goal formulations, both the fundamental goals of Norwegian security policy and the formulation of the Armed Forces' goal structure, are in full accordance with the overall joint allied perspectives that Norway has endorsed in connection with NATO's adaptation to the new Europe

[1354] It is also important that they fully grasp the new security policy challenges and tasks that have a direct or indirect bearing on our country's security policy position in the years to come

[1355] The fundamental security policy goals that form the basis for the Armed Forces' tasks are

[1356] to prevent war and contribute to stability and peaceful development; - to protect Norwegian freedom of action against political and military pressure, and safeguard Norwegian rights and interests; - to defend Norwegian land, sea and air territory against violation and attack

[1357] For a more detailed discussion of the goals and tasks of the Norwegian Armed Forces, see chapters 5.1 and

[1358] DEFENSE POLICY AND MILITARY FRAMEWORK CONDITIONS

[1359] Defense capability and combat capability

[1360] The goal of Norwegian security policy is national security

[1361] However, safeguarding Norwegian security interests requires that the security interests of other countries are also safeguarded

[1362] Common security ensures national security

[1363] National security can be more easily promoted if international developments are characterized by greater stability and fewer challenges and threats

[1364] Norwegian security is therefore strengthened through active and direct international engagement, where Norway, together with other countries, not just allies, seeks common solutions to common problems

[1365] The concept of national security basically encompasses all aspects of safeguarding Norwegian security interests

[1366] Therefore, the Armed Forces constitute one of several security policy instruments

[1367] In a broader sense, national security will be a function of Norway's political, economic and military relations with the outside world

[1368] In principle, situations could be imagined where Norway's military capacity has marginal significance for the country's security situation as a whole, as long as the country has secured its security interests through economic and political measures and cooperation arrangements and obtained the necessary guarantees and support from other countries, so that military aggression from third countries no longer appears likely or is affected by changes in Norway's military capacity

[1369] The realities of the 1990s, however, indicate that Norwegian security cannot be based exclusively on political and economic ties and cooperation with other countries, but that the need for protection against unpredictable challenges and threats must still be met also with the help of military forces

[1370] It is therefore important to safeguard national security in a defense policy sense

[1371] In this sense, national security combines

[1372] Norway's defense capability with the probability of war or use of armed force

[1373] There is a complex relationship between these two factors

[1374] Too low a defense capability can affect the likelihood of the use of armed force against Norway, but a number of other factors may also play a role

[1375] For a more detailed description and assessment of these factors, see Chapter

[1376] It is desirable to use concepts that provide an opportunity to assess what constitutes national security in a defense policy sense

[1377] It is therefore necessary to make a distinction between defensive capability and combat capability

[1378] It is also desirable to assess the connection between security policy developments and the Armed Forces' ability to carry out its tasks

[1379] This requires a clarification of the two concepts

[1380] Defense capability is linked to the Armed Forces' ability to solve its primary military tasks in war, i.e. provide the strongest possible resistance to any form of attack, assert sovereignty over Norwegian territory, and be able to quickly repel, limit or defeat various forms of aggression

[1381] When assessing the defense capability, three factors in particular will come into play

[1382] The combat capability of the Norwegian Armed Forces

[1383] Allied reinforcements' combat capability

[1384] The combat capability of the military forces that can be deployed in operations directed at Norwegian territory in the event of war

[1385] Combat capability can be divided into combat value and combat endurance

[1386] Combat value says something about how well equipped the military units appear, including personnel, materiel and combat facilities

[1387] This value depends on both quantitative and qualitative factors, including geography and terrain where they are expected to operate in their missions

[1388] Combat endurance is primarily dependent on the logistics apparatus, including stocks of combat materiel (fuel, ammunition, spare parts, etc

[1389] Changes in combat capability can, to a certain extent, be assessed as a combination of qualitative and quantitative factors of importance to the combat value and combat endurance of military units within a given force structure

[1390] This is a situation that Norway itself has an influence on through the resources that are made available to the Armed Forces, and through the way these resources are managed

[1391] Secondly, Norwegian defense must be seen in the context of the alliance

[1392] Several factors will come into play here; our allies' ability and willingness to support Norway and secondly how the Norwegian side facilitates, supports and cooperates with allied units

[1393] The third element in this context is the combat capability of the forces that would potentially be deployed against Norway

[1394] For Norway, in the post-war period, this has revolved around the Soviet Union's military capacity in the north

[1395] After the upheavals since 1989/90, this element has changed

[1396] Russia is not the Soviet Union, and seeks political and economic partnership with Western countries

[1397] At the same time, it is difficult to assess to what extent the legacy from the old system can still be felt

[1398] The uncertainty surrounding the question of where Russia is headed makes it difficult to assess what military capacity the country will have in a few years

[1399] The country is in an unstable transition phase, characterized by a fluid process somewhere between democracy and dictatorship, and strong factions are competing over the country's future political course

[1400] For Norway, it will be of primary interest to follow the development of forces in the northwestern parts of Russia

[1401] Even if political developments in Russia were to move in a favorable direction, setbacks cannot be ruled out

[1402] The increasing instability and power struggle within Russia reinforces this assessment

[1403] Consequently, potential future military operations against Norway cannot be ruled out

[1404] When assessing defense and combat capabilities, it will therefore be necessary to take due account of the uncertainty of future developments

[1405] From the Norwegian side, emphasis must be placed on the existing military capacity in Russia

[1406] The design of Norway's future defense must be based on the fact that political objectives can change quickly, that existing military capacity can be used in new and unexpected ways, and that military strength and competence require time and practice to maintain and build

[1407] Clarifying what the Armed Forces' goals are must form the basis for determining what the Armed Forces will produce and for assessing whether the Armed Forces are prioritizing the use of resources correctly

[1408] Once it has been determined what the Armed Forces will produce over a given period, management will need to be geared towards ensuring that production takes place as efficiently as possible

[1409] This assumes that the value creation in the entire defense organization can be described, which, among other things, assumes the above mentioned distinction between defense and combat capability

[1410] The end products are the benefits that society expects to receive from the Armed Forces, and for which the Storting allocates funds

[1411] Combat capability is the end product of the Armed Forces' own value creation in relation to the Armed Forces' tasks in crisis and war

[1412] Like defense capability, combat capability is linked to a situation where Norway is exposed to military aggression

[1413] The product cannot be measured in peace

[1414] The end product in peace therefore appears to be the production apparatus that, together with other non-measurable variables such as leadership and morale, creates combat capability

[1415] It is the quality of the war structure and support apparatus that produces combat capability

[1416] As is clear from the report, the Norwegian Armed Forces' war structure, peacekeeping organization and activities are undergoing extensive restructuring

[1417] The decisions and measures that will be implemented as a result of this report will have a major influence on the development of Norway's combat capability

[1418] In Chapter 6, the effects on combat and defense capabilities of the specific proposed changes to the organization and activities of the Armed Forces will be discussed in more detail

[1419] Political changes and a new military situation in Europe

[1420] The extensive political changes in Europe in recent years have also led to changes in the sizing, structuring and deployment of military forces

[1421] New military contacts are being established between countries in Eastern and Western Europe

[1422] New arms control measures must be developed and implemented

[1423] From the Western side, it is a goal that the military force structure and activities of the former Warsaw Pact countries change towards becoming more similar to Western countries through negotiations, dialogue and closer cooperation

[1612] Developments beyond the 1990s will change the stable picture of Norway's military-strategic importance and of the challenges and threats the country will face

[1613] The old two-part world has been replaced by an unclear world where challenges can come from unexpected quarters

Since 1989, the combined military capacity on the Soviet and later Russian side in the north - i.e. within the Leningrad and Baltic military districts

[1617] LEMD and BAMD) - have been markedly reduced

[1618] The reduced capacity in the north is the result of several factors; a generally lower level of tension also in the north, disarmament agreements concluded, and internal economic problems and reorganization needs as a result of the Russian forces adapting to a new international situation

[1619] The reductions have taken the form of both personnel and material reductions, but perhaps most importantly is a somewhat significant decrease in the scope of exercises and operability

[1620] These reductions do not alter the great strategic importance of the LEMD and especially the Kola region for Russian defense planning, even into the 1990s

[1621] Russia is smaller in size and population than the former Soviet Union, and at the same time the country's geographical center of gravity has shifted further east and north, with the ice-free ports on the Kola Peninsula as the only free access westward to the open sea

[1622] In line with Ukrainian and Baltic independence, the importance of the Black Sea and Baltic Fleets for Russian defense planning has been greatly reduced

[1623] The Kola region will constitute Russia's main home base for sea-based strategic systems and will be of vital importance for the air defense of Russian territory

[1624] These two main functions in themselves indicate that Russia will maintain a significant presence of both strategic and various types of conventional forces in the LEMD

[1625] There are already signs that the northern region will be given priority in future Russian defense planning

[1626] Force reductions in the area are actively sought to be combined with consolidation of remaining forces

[2151] The defense of Norway must not only be viewed against the background of Norway's own defense capabilities and military capacity, but also in light of allied reinforcements and allied countries' ability and willingness to transfer forces to Norway in a crisis or conflict situation

[2152] Norway's membership in NATO has had and will continue to have a decisive impact on ensuring that a fight over Norwegian territory is not limited to a fight only against Norwegian military units

[2153] However, the rapid process of change in international politics means that familiar patterns of alliance cooperation can quickly shift

[2155] The alliance will remain, but the nature of allied cooperation will be influenced, among other things, by the development of a separate EC-based European defense identity, the relationship between the United States and the EC, and the relationship between the United States and the European great powers

[2166] But the individual country's political forms of cooperation with other allied countries will also increasingly have an impact on whether these allied countries will contribute to the respective alliance country's defense

[2184] Allied reinforcements Allied reinforcements are of crucial importance for the defense of Norway

[2185] Reinforcements form an essential part of the alliance's defense planning

[2186] A Norwegian defense force can stop a first invasion attempt on its own

[2187] Maintaining a balanced defense with invasion defense capabilities in a region of the country will ensure this

[2188] However, such a defense alone will not be able to maintain control for a long time under sustained pressure

[2210] The European NATO countries will have to take greater responsibility for the defense of their own territories

[2225] The value of air combat forces is increasing for modern warfare, and the dependence on future allied combat aircraft must be seen, among other things, in the light of the fact that this announcement does not intend to increase the number of combat aircraft beyond the number Norway currently has at its disposal

[2228] It is also a question of creating conditions for the reception and support of allied reinforcements

[2232] The decision concerns limited supply support, and is under review in NATO bodies

[2233] Such supply support will represent a continuation of similar measures that have previously been implemented in Norway

[2235] From the Norwegian side, it is planned that allied reinforcements will continue to constitute a significant part of the defense plans for Norway

[2236] The planning of the Norwegian force structure for the period ahead will be based on allied reinforcement forces covering the same functions as previously

[2238] Allied cooperation - joint exercises To underpin the credibility of defence cooperation within NATO, it is still necessary for allied reinforcement forces to learn about the Norwegian climate and terrain through exercises in Norway

[2239] There will be a need to practice receiving and deploying allied forces

[2240] As a result of NATO's new strategy, force structure and reinforcement concept with increased emphasis on flexibility and crisis management, an adaptation effort is currently underway in NATO that will also have an impact on the established exercise pattern in Norway

[2241] The development of the allied exercise pattern will be of great importance to Norway, and at the same time represent an indication of the direction in which Western defense and security cooperation is heading

[2242] The shift in focus away from the High North could have an impact on the alliance's willingness to prioritize Norway in the context of exercises

[2243] Should developments in Russia go in an unfortunate direction, this will affect the attention of allied countries directed towards the High North

[2245] The system for allied exercise planning that affects Norway and the High North must therefore be designed so that Norwegian security interests can also be safeguarded in such a light

[2246] Allied participation in exercise activities in Norway is still characterized by the previous exercise pattern; partly in the form of allied exercises, and partly allied participation in national exercises

[2247] The exercise pattern in the latter half of the 1980s was characterized by large cyclical variations

[2248] Out of consideration for the strain on the receiving apparatus, planning capacity and the environment, Norway, in consultation with its allies after 1990, came to a more even distribution over time of the large NATO exercises with field participation

[2249] The exercise pattern since 1992 has thus been characterized by only one major exercise with field participation each year, alternating between Team Work, Battle Griffin and Express

[2250] Battle Griffin was first conducted in 1991 as a new series of exercises with the purpose of practicing the deployment concept for an airborne US Marine Infantry Brigade (MEB) as part of NATO's reinforcement plan with the Northern Region as the deployment area

[2252] The Express exercises are conducted each time in Northern Norway, with the participation of NATO's Mobile Force (AMF) and other allied and national units

[2253] The naval exercises Northern Wedding and Ocean Safari were replaced towards the end of the 1980s by a new series of exercises, North Star, with the aim of ensuring a major allied naval exercise in the Norwegian Sea each year with the participation of, among other things, American aircraft carriers

[2254] The exercise was first carried out

[2277] Division of labor and role specialization

[2278] As the defense budgets of several member states are reduced, while quality requirements combined with expensive new technology make it difficult for small alliance countries to maintain all the main components of a modern defense, the question of division of labor and role specialization may become more relevant

[2279] The trend towards increased use of multinational forces, as envisaged by NATO's new strategy and force structure, also makes it more relevant to consider the division of labor in a new light

[2280] To the extent that the future conventional force structure is implemented, a more closely integrated alliance defense, built around a core of multinational forces, will increasingly be able to rely on a certain degree of division of labor, including in the form of role specialization

[2281] The question in this regard is to what extent it is realistic to expect that affected countries will accept a functional division of labor

[2282] It is unlikely that the respective countries, perhaps especially the great powers, will accept an arrangement in which certain military tasks are fully given to other allied states

[2283] In that case, one will be dependent on another country's acceptance, for example for the use of fighter aircraft, or for the use of certain types of vessels

[2284] The question is therefore where the limit for the division of labor will be set

[2285] It can be expected that a sober level of ambition in this context can be set and pursued, where emphasis will be placed on building on a core of multinational units

[2286] Beyond this, most countries, not least the major powers, will probably prioritize maintaining balanced forces, in the sense that they will be able to handle all essential military functions themselves

[2287] However, this situation does not have to conflict with these countries' desire to allocate units to multinational forces and purposes

[2288] For European major powers, it may therefore be appropriate to divide labor within a narrower, firmly defined framework, e.g. the development of forces that can operate under WEU auspices, while the countries simultaneously maintain balanced national forces, which are not earmarked for efforts in areas where division of labor seems appropriate

[2289] However, the issue of division of labor is primarily relevant for smaller countries

[2290] Scarce own resources combined with new tasks or new requirements for equipment and quality link the issue to small countries

[2291] Should the EU countries expand the WEU in such a way that a clearer military division of labor is made possible within the framework of an overall, closely integrated political cooperation within the EC, the smaller EC countries will be able to more directly assess to what extent and in what way their own national forces should be built up as part of a closely coordinated European defense

[2292] If so, the opportunity will increase to investigate new defense concepts that are no longer based on national, balanced forces

[2293] In this context, it is important to recognize that a process that points clearly in this direction is already well underway

[2294] During the 1993-98 planning period, the issue of allied division of labor could have progressed significantly

[2295] The future development of WEU could therefore have a major impact on future patterns of allied military cooperation

[2296] Closer political integration linked to the EC and WEU could mean that the issue of division of labor and role specialization becomes more relevant

[2297] The connection between, on the one hand, what each allied country can contribute to the common defense, and in what way this should best be done, and, on the other hand, what tasks it is desired on a national basis that its own military forces should be able to perform, will be central

[2298] The consideration of a nationally balanced defense is, among other things, linked to the goal of maintaining an invasion defense

[2299] To the extent that other countries are assigned specific tasks, and a country itself renounces force elements that can carry out these tasks, the country's defense will be part of an integrated allied defense

[2300] If the country is to be able to establish an invasion defense, this will have to be seen as a function of the extent to which other allied countries involved prioritize this country's security interests, territory, and neighboring areas

[2301] The issue of division of labor and role specialization is therefore very complex in nature and affects significant and sensitive national issues

[2302] The discussion about burden sharing; about the distribution of responsibilities, risks and tasks, has characterized NATO for many years

[2303] Following the upheavals in Europe, a new burden-sharing debate is underway, where the issue is what should be a reasonable burden-sharing between the United States and the European countries regarding the defense of Europe

[2304] In the United States, many have believed that the country has contributed disproportionately to the defense of allied countries

[2305] American public opinion seems to view with increasing skepticism the United States' military involvement in Europe, as we know it from the post-war period

[2306] Budget deficits and the general economic situation in the United States also support this trend

[2307] The Clinton administration will review the United States' political and economic engagement and commitments in light of key international developments and the role the administration wants the United States to play

[2308] Europeans will increasingly have to contribute to the defense of Europe

[2309] In parallel with - and as a result of - this development, the development of the EU countries' security and defense policy cooperation is underway

[2310] In this context, the question of the future scope of North American and European reinforcements will be addressed

[2311] The United States will continue to be Norway's primary security guarantor, but Norway's relationship with the EU and WEU also has significant defense and security significance

[2312] The American proposal to change the financing scheme for allied installations in Europe must also be seen in this context

[2313] The system of joint financing via the infrastructure budget that is now being proposed may involve a shift of spending from the American side to the European side

[2314] This could mean, among other things, that maintenance during pre-storage is borne by the individual host country

[2315] A decision in principle has been made in NATO that operating costs related to installations and facilities in Europe intended for American reinforcements should be jointly financed, but that such costs should compete on an equal footing with other projects

[2316] Whether there will actually be a shift in spending will therefore become a question of priority

[2317] The financial framework within which the Allied Reinforcement Installations scheme operates makes it difficult in the short term to obtain funds for the implementation of joint financing

[2318] In any event, the content of the US reinforcement commitments is subject to assessment

[2319] The outcome of the United States' reassessment of its commitments in Europe may help raise the question of a possible closer allied division of labor in Europe, which will also affect the Norwegian Armed Forces

[2320] Norwegian participation in NATO's multinational forces The Alliance's new strategy and force concept places increased emphasis on multinational forces in which as many member states as possible participate

[2321] The government has decided that Norway will contribute to NATO's new emergency response forces with units from all branches of defense

[2322] This means that Norwegian forces from both the army, air force and navy, as part of the alliance's multinational forces, will be able to be deployed in operations outside Norway

[2323] Norwegian participation in the Alliance's multinational forces does not, in principle, represent any new obligations in relation to those that Norway has already undertaken as a NATO member, including adherence to the Alliance's integrated military cooperation

[2324] There will be an opportunity to reassess each country's force contribution to multinational forces annually in connection with NATO's force planning process

[2325] On the naval side, Norway is scheduled to participate to approximately the same extent as Norway currently participates in both the standing naval forces in the Atlantic and the Channel, and in support of SACLANT in the form of routine surveillance and patrolling in the northern sea areas

[2326] It will therefore primarily be about continuing the current commitment

[2327] The naval participation will include both rapid and immediate response forces

[2328] In total, it may be appropriate to participate with two escort vessels, two minelayers, four submarines, four maritime patrol aircraft and two reconnaissance aircraft

[2329] Regarding the air force, it is intended that Norway will participate with a squadron of F-16 fighter aircraft in the immediate response forces

[2330] In this regard, cooperation with Denmark is being considered

[2331] Regarding the army, Norway will contribute an infantry battalion to the forces for immediate response

[2332] Various options are being worked on regarding how participation on the army side should be organized

[2333] Participation in the multinational forces will entail some additional operating costs, especially as a result of increased exercise activity together with corresponding units from other NATO countries

[2334] In addition, there will be certain investment expenditures related to equipment for the army and air force

[2335] These are related to the need for standardization in order to operate together with departments from other countries

[2336] A prerequisite has been that the multinational emergency response forces in a given situation should also be deployed in conflicts within the alliance's traditional area of responsibility

[2337] The emergency forces will be part of the alliance's overall defense capacity, and could potentially be deployed in a conflict as part of the alliance's collective defense, cf. Article 5 of the Atlantic Charter

[2338] A decision on the deployment of NATO's emergency response forces will have to be made in NATO's Defense Planning Committee, i.e. at government level, in the same way as with the use of other forces under NATO auspices

[2339] Against the background of the general tendency for key international organizations to become more closely linked, overlap and complement each other, NATO countries have opened up the possibility of the alliance making its military organization and selected forces available outside the territory of the alliance countries

[2340] NATO forces will be able to be used in peacekeeping operations outside NATO's traditional area of responsibility under the auspices and with a mandate from the CSCE or the UN

[2341] However, it will be up to each country to decide on its participation in such peacekeeping operations

[2342] The Norwegian units that will be part of the alliance's multinational forces will also be able to be used in this type of mission if it is deemed appropriate in a given situation

[2343] It will not be possible to base participation in the IRF (Immediate Response Force) with an infantry battalion on the use of mobilization personnel

[2344] Norwegian participation therefore requires the recruitment of volunteers among those subject to military service, where some additional service will be required

[2345] This could provide the army with specialized expertise that will be important also as the period of conscription has been reduced and changed in accordance with the guidelines recommended by FK

[2346] A Norwegian IRF battalion will likely entail some additional operating costs and investment costs related to new necessary equipment

[2347] A Norwegian IRF unit must be able to operate together with other allied units, this requires, among other things, a certain degree of standardization, also with regard to the level of materiel

[2348] The maritime emergency response force STANAVFORLANT may also be subject to new requirements for operations and equipment

[2349] As participation of Norwegian personnel in multinational operations abroad will be based exclusively on volunteerism, the Ministry will, as the pattern for deployment of Norwegian units and departments in such operations becomes clearer, consider in more detail which criteria will apply to voluntary deployment in such emergency forces, who will be able to be recruited for such deployment and what conditions will be applied

[2350] Many new conventional weapons systems can be delivered with great efficiency from aircraft

[2351] Air combat and control of airspace are becoming increasingly important for modern warfare

[2352] Air warfare and the air force have therefore increasingly become a dominant factor in conventional warfare

[2353] Through extensive and concentrated air warfare, one can strike the opposing party's command and control apparatus, isolate theaters of operations by cutting off communications to the area where the conflict is being decided, carry out strategic bombing of the opposing party's infrastructure, industrial plants and resources, and weaken the opposing party's mobilization and establishment of reserve forces

[2354] Through such air warfare, the prerequisites for a modern, highly mobile battle are established, where ground forces and naval forces are used in combined operations together with air forces with the aim of achieving rapid decisions through the concentration of flexible forces

[2355] A minimum air defense seems to form the basis for the efforts of the other defense branches

[2356] Some of the wars that have been fought over the past couple of decades have provided some experiences that can contribute to the basis for Norwegian defense planning

[2357] Certain lessons from the Gulf War, the Falklands War, and the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan have provided insight into important aspects of modern warfare

[2358] These wars were fought under conditions that in most areas are significantly different from the conditions that would characterize military conflict in Norway

[2359] For example, the Gulf War was fought after a long period of preparation, which provided a high level of training, far higher than if a conflict were to come more unexpectedly and forces were deployed into combat more quickly

[2360] Experience with the effectiveness of weapons at the time must also be balanced against the impact of expected future countermeasures

[2361] The experiences from these wars cannot therefore be directly transferred

[2362] However, some observations have more general validity

[2363] The 1991 Gulf War demonstrated the crucial importance that air superiority and the use of advanced air-delivered weapons can have both for a country's overall armed defense capability and for the course of the land conflict itself

[2364] The coalition's air forces neutralized Iraq's air defenses very quickly through a coordinated effort against the command and control apparatus, the air stations, and the few aircraft that managed to enter combat

[2365] It was not primarily an insufficient number of aircraft, but limitations and vulnerabilities in the support apparatus that were the cause of Iraq's defeat in the air war

[2366] Full air control gave the coalition's air forces free rein to carry out extensive airstrikes that over time had decisive consequences for the further course of the war

[2367] The Iraqi combat command apparatus was neutralized, the land theater itself isolated, and the land forces exposed to attacks that resulted in extensive casualties, desertion, and a breakdown in morale

[2368] At the same time, the coalition suffered remarkably few casualties, given the large forces deployed on both sides

[2369] The defeat of Iraq was achieved through a combined effort of advanced weapons and large quantities of conventional weapons

[2370] The land dispute itself was very short-lived

[2371] The battle was decided through extensive maneuvering by coalition forces, concentration of force, and brief confrontations with Iraqi units, many of which had very limited combat capabilities

[2372] The Allied naval presence was extensive during the war, as were the naval operations

[2373] A large part of Iraq's navy was destroyed by coalition anti-ship missiles

[2374] Ship-based combat aircraft and cruise missiles formed an important part of the coalition's combat effort

[2375] The most important experience on the maritime side is related to the extensive naval transfers of forces, equipment and logistics from the United States and Western Europe to the area of operations

[2376] The vast majority of these large transfers had to be made by sea, and the operation would have been very risky without naval control in the waters outside the operational area

[2377] However, the Iraqis managed to hinder some coalition operations by using traditional, simple mines

[2378] This illustrates the great potential that lies in such relatively simple and cheap mines when they are used in a way that creates uncertainty

[2379] On the operational and tactical level, the Gulf War clearly demonstrated the importance of integrated combat management, in addition to the major consequences that can be achieved by denying the opposing party good situational awareness and the dissemination of important information

[2380] In this context, the coalition forces' superiority in electronic warfare was a very important factor

[2381] Electronic warfare has become increasingly important in modern warfare

[2382] The underdog in such electronic warfare can quickly find themselves in a very difficult military situation

[2383] Units that lose the ability to act in a coordinated manner and utilize their weapons and sensors quickly lose both morale, combat power, and ability/will to continue fighting

[2384] Modern forces must therefore have the ability to operate in a combat environment characterized by electronic warfare measures

[2385] Another factor of great importance during this conflict was the use of weapons with great precision and penetration that could quickly knock out important static targets

[2386] The problems the coalition air forces had in neutralizing the mobile Iraqi SCUD batteries provide a good indication of the strength that can be found in mobile system concepts

[2387] Against this background, such mobile weapons systems can have a great effect as a threat and blackmail factor, and in combat can tie down relatively large forces

[2388] The training standard of the forces deployed by the coalition was high

[2389] This proved to be an important factor that contributed greatly to the outcome of the war

[2390] Intensive training programs over several months proved necessary even for forces with professional crews

[2391] Many of the mobilizable American combat units were considered less effective than the professionals and were not deployed in direct combat

[2392] Experience indicates that the combination of suitable equipment and well-trained crews creates opportunities for effective defensive combat in a modern combat environment

[2393] Personnel with a high level of education and training will be able to more effectively utilize the potential inherent in modern weapons systems and combinations thereof

[2394] The ability to see in the dark and in bad weather, in addition to the fast pace of combat, means that modern warfare can be fought very intensively and continuously throughout the day

[2395] This places high demands on personnel and equipment

[2396] Opportunities for rest are reduced, and the need for replacements during double shifts of personnel increases

[2397] The Gulf War also demonstrated how strongly the presence and risk of use of weapons of mass destruction affects all aspects of both the preparation for and conduct of a war

[2398] The war in Afghanistan gave the Soviet forces considerable experience in operations in mountainous terrain with poorly developed communications against a lightly equipped and mobile opponent

[2399] Doctrines and tactics as well as the need for platforms and weapons were developed during the war

[2400] In particular, the operations provided experience in the extensive use of helicopters for transport and attack

[2401] The warfare was otherwise characterized by the widespread use of anti-personnel mines and extensive destruction of civilian infrastructure

[2402] Russian forces must today be assumed to have relatively extensive experience in this type of operations against forces of a completely different nature than the heavily equipped, regular forces they were trained to operate against in Central Europe

[2403] The conditions in Norway are in many ways very different, and defense of Norwegian territory will not be conducted in the same way as the guerrilla forces operated in Afghanistan, even though the terrain in parts of Norway has significant similarities

[2404] The experiences from Afghanistan are primarily relevant to the extent that they have influenced the Russian forces' equipment, doctrine and tactics for combat under similar conditions

[2405] The land battle in the Falkland Islands provided little guidance for Norwegian defense planning, except for the general experience that the British forces' ability to act tactically offensively and mobilely contributed significantly to their victory

[2406] The British tactical helicopter operations followed by combat patrols and night attacks did not give the Argentines peace and ultimately broke their fighting morale

[2407] The Argentine defense of the Falklands was static and inflexible, similar to how the Iraqi forces acted during the Gulf War

[2408] Another important factor that also played a role during both conflicts was the high standard of training on one of the two warring sides

[2409] During the Falklands conflict, the Argentine soldiers were essentially poorly trained conscripts

[2410] This not only contributed to their defeat, but also caused relatively heavy losses

[2411] The Falklands War demonstrated the importance of being able to confront an adversary with a multifaceted threat

[2412] The British deployed large resources, including a large number of helicopters, to protect the aircraft carriers against the perceived Argentine submarine threat

[2413] An adapted and flexible capability for early air warning proved to be very important

[2414] The radar systems were adapted for operations in open waters and therefore did not work satisfactorily in coastal waters

[2415] Argentine fighter planes in several cases fired their missiles before the planes were detected, and the British loss of ships was largely due to a lack of air warning of incoming fighter planes and missiles, in addition to the fact that the British were forced to use some surface ships as radar stations for advance warning, which made these vessels very vulnerable

[2416] The naval operations during the Falklands War demonstrated, among other things, the importance of conventional submarines and their potential in waters characterized by high acoustic noise and consistently poor visibility, high winds and high seas

[2417] Such conditions are similar to those in the waters off the Norwegian coast

[2418] Under these conditions, effective anti-submarine operations can be prevented or made more difficult, among other things because the performance of ship-based sonar systems is reduced and ship-based helicopters that are to conduct operations against submarines cannot take off

[2419] The ability of conventional submarines to threaten or tie down the opposing party's naval forces in such coastal waters is relevant to Norway

[2420] Air control was believed to be crucial during the British landing

[2421] British attempts to neutralize the Argentine Air Force failed

[2422] This posed a significant operational risk

[2423] Had the Argentines launched airstrikes against the landing operations instead of against British naval vessels, the course of the battle could have been different

[2424] For Norwegian defense planning, this experience illustrates the importance of being able to maintain acceptable endurance and survivability in the components that are intended to deter or defend the country against sea invasion

[2425] The Falklands War demonstrated how considerations of survival and low vulnerability can be deprioritized during a long period of peace

[2426] The fatal outcome of the air attacks on several British naval vessels was due to fires on board

[2427] Despite experiences from World War II and knowledge acquired through research, flammable materials were used and safety measures were neglected aboard British naval vessels

[2428] However, the vessels completed their task, and showed that even though naval forces cannot be secured against all conceivable threats, and losses must therefore be expected under all circumstances, modern vessels can still contribute to achieving the set political goals in a war

[2429] Armed conflicts fought over the past 20 years show that military technology has had a pervasive impact on all aspects of modern warfare

[2430] A general consequence seems to be that modern technology can to a greater extent have an "all or nothing" effect on the outcome of military operations

[2431] This is especially true where operations are in the nature of a duel between technically advanced systems where the overall weapon effect depends not only on the quality of the weapon itself, but also on the associated sensors, communications equipment, platforms, etc

[2432] The quality of the personnel is also important

[2433] While there was previously room to compensate for major material quality differences with better training, superior organization and tactics, etc., developments seem to make approximate technological parity between the warring parties more important

[2434] It seems that even modest differences in technological level under certain conditions can have significant consequences

[2435] A modern combat environment thus represents new conditions for armed combat, especially if regular units and forces fight against each other

[2436] Military-technological development Over the past few decades, military-technical development has progressed rapidly and led to significantly higher performance from one generation of equipment to the next

[2437] Development has taken place on a broad front and included surveillance and detection systems, platforms, weapons and fire control systems

[2438] Many of the major advances that have been made are due to the use of computer technology, often in combination with modern sensor technology

[2439] Significant improvements in performance have simultaneously created new operational opportunities and, in the long term, lead to changes in organization, operational and tactical doctrine, leadership styles, and ultimately also to a restructuring of national military strategies

[2440] Within the area of strategic surveillance, satellites with modern observation tools are becoming an essential supplement to more traditional methods

[2441] Such satellites make it possible to monitor military activities and force movements

[2442] They will therefore play an important role both in the ability to verify disarmament and arms control agreements and in the ability to provide strategic warning about military force buildup

[2443] When it comes to tactical surveillance, sensor, communications and data technology also creates the basis for significant performance improvements

[2444] Weather and light-independent sensors provide opportunities to continuously monitor the opponent's dispositions and make good decisions about your own efforts at the right time

[2445] A characteristic of the development of conventional weapons is that many such weapons systems are given the ability to reach their targets with high precision

[2446] This can be combined with long range and good ability to penetrate physical protection

[2447] Such weapons will primarily be used against high-priority, static targets

[2448] For use against mobile targets, strict requirements are placed on fire control

[2449] Technological developments in sensors, communications, data processing and satellites offer great potential for improvement

[2450] Continued significant investment in these technology areas is expected

[2451] Also against dense concentrations of moving targets, highly effective area weapons are under development, where each of the many small arms in the system has an independent ability to detect and attack individual targets

[2452] Such weapons will mainly be air-delivered, and pose a new and serious threat to land forces

[2453] New methods for protecting combat vehicles are being developed and implemented

[2454] This makes previous generations of anti-tank weapons ineffective and creates a need for the development of new anti-tank technology

[2455] Similarly, the increased threat from air-delivered weapons will create a need for air defense systems with significantly improved performance

[2456] A key aspect of further development in all these areas will be to find technology that provides acceptable performance at the lowest possible price

[2457] Systems based on modern electronic technology are highly effective, but also open the door to electronic countermeasures

[2458] If such are developed and purposefully used in combat, the effectiveness of the opposing side's weapons systems can be dramatically reduced

[2459] Electronic countermeasure technology is thus a response to the development of new weapons technology

[2460] It often requires detailed knowledge of the counterparty's systems, and the effectiveness of countermeasures is conditional on their mode of operation not being known to the other party

[2461] Technology related to electronic countermeasures is therefore often subject to strict secrecy

[2462] However, the possibility of using electronic countermeasures directly as a means of warfare opens up interesting perspectives for a small country like Norway, with significant electronic expertise and industry

[2463] Western military forces have so far generally had better weapons and support systems than former Warsaw Pact countries, due to the generally higher technological level in the West

[2464] In some areas where advanced computer technology was central, the time advantage could be up to ten years

[2465] In other fields, the Soviet systems were on par with Western ones and often had their strength in robustness, reliability, and ease of use

[2466] The Soviet force structure and doctrine took into account, among other things, a lower level of education and acceptance of a potentially greater loss of personnel

[2467] In the post-war period, the forces of the former Warsaw Pact countries included several generations of weapons systems with very different levels of technology and performance

[2468] This situation is now rapidly changing

[2469] It is therefore difficult to give a general assessment of the difference between military capabilities in Eastern and Western Europe

[2470] The development and acquisition of new generations of advanced weapons requires large resources

[2471] The economic capacity of states and the prioritization of military defense therefore have great importance for how quickly and to what extent new technology can be incorporated into military forces

[2472] The pace of development and phasing in of new weapons systems will also in all likelihood be reduced

[2473] Despite the major political changes that have occurred, everything indicates that the Russian authorities also emphasize the importance of modern technology in the development of their military forces

[2474] The agreements that have been concluded on arms control and disarmament do not set any limits on research and development activity, or on the quality and performance of materiel

[2475] It is also clear that the least advanced equipment will only be withdrawn when the former Warsaw Pact countries are to reduce their deployments in accordance with the CFE-1 treaty's force limits

[2476] There is every reason to believe that Russia will seek to maintain an effective defense

[2477] It is still uncertain how Russia will prioritize defense development and production

[2478] The internal power struggle will affect the importance given to the country's military forces, but so far there have been several signals that the military sector is still prioritized

[2479] The size of the Russian military forces will likely be significantly reduced, but new technology will likely be developed and applied in areas that are important for the forces' ability to fight effectively in a modern combat environment

[2480] reduced resources for military defense in Western countries, very significant savings will have to be made in connection with the acquisition of new equipment

[2481] However, there is much evidence of a continued focus on furthering military-technological development in all important fields

[2482] This will likely lead to sustained military research and development efforts in the United States and most major Western European countries

[2483] The bulk of the savings will be achieved through reduced scope and pace associated with the actual phasing in of new equipment

[2484] This raises a difficult question about how production capacity and associated expertise can be maintained at a sufficiently high level in view of any increasing future demand

[2485] It takes a very long time to build such expertise and capacity from scratch

[2486] The general technological development for the civilian sector in Western countries will continue at a rapid pace

[2487] Technology developed for civilian purposes will also be used in military products to a much greater extent

[2488] This curbs the growth in costs associated with the development of new products, while the interaction between the civilian and military sectors contributes to the pace of technological development

[2489] Consequences of military-technical development Today's performance level for modern war material primarily provides opportunities for operations with a completely different intensity and continuity than previously

[2490] Equipment for observation and firing in the dark turns night into day and has enabled 24/7 maneuvering and combat

[2491] Modern communications equipment enables rapid and encrypted transmission of intelligence, orders and directives, with rapid concentration of force at the point where a decision is sought

[2492] The modular principle simplifies the technical maintenance of complex equipment used in the front line, as entire components can be replaced in a short time during combat

[2493] New technology in weapons and support systems has made it possible to conduct military operations very effectively and achieve operational objectives quickly, provided that the adversary does not have suitable countermeasures and weapons systems at a fairly comparable level of performance

[2494] Good alignment between the characteristics of new weapons systems and the strategic and tactical doctrines that underpin warfare will increasingly appear to be important

[2495] Based on the system capabilities of modern weapons technology, a fundamental shift in the concept of effective conventional warfare is about to occur

[2496] A concept based on a war of attrition with heavy casualties over long periods of combat, where the emphasis is on the size of the forces rather than flexibility, gives way to a concept where a battle decision can be achieved in an early phase of the war with an emphasis on maneuver warfare and flexible force deployment aimed at the opponent's weak points

[2497] In theory, such a combat concept represents nothing new, but the weapons development of the last decade has given it new content

[2498] Consequences for management and training standards

[2499] Dynamic combat with an emphasis on maneuver, flexibility, and concentration of firepower places strict demands on overview and combat management

[2500] It is likely that the minimum factor for effective combat with modern weapons will be good combat leadership

[2501] In this field, sensor and data technology opens up new possibilities

[2502] However, the development of systems for decision support and for command and control with the implementation of extensive operations has still not nearly exploited the potential that could lie in the technology itself

[2503] The main problem is extracting essential information and making it available in an appropriate form as a basis for ongoing decisions

[2504] Vulnerability is another critical factor

[2505] It will be possible to promote effective combat management and the effective use of one's own forces if computer systems are utilized appropriately in an exercise context

[2506] Computer-supported staff exercises, for example, could have significant training and financial gain potential in the longer term, among other things because the staff apparatus can be trained more realistically by computer-based simulators providing real time feedback on the effects of the staff's decisions in selected scenarios

[2507] It will also be possible to run through planned exercises in advance, thereby giving conscripts more effective exercises and thus better training within a shorter time

[2508] The need to practice maneuver elements in the terrain will be reduced

[2509] This has socio-economic effects

[2510] Computer-based systems for command, control and exercises are resource-intensive

[2511] Norway has established cooperation with other allies within the framework of NATO to exploit the benefits such systems can provide economically and operationally

[2512] The growing dynamics and the periodically very high pace of modern warfare place strict demands on the training standards of personnel

[2513] This applies at all levels of the military organization, but is particularly important for combat management and for the effective use of complex systems in integrated operations

[2514] The high intensity of combat will also put both the crews' technical skills and fighting morale to the test

[2515] The demands on the individual soldier and unit are also increasing, both in relation to the operation of weapons and equipment and to general physical and mental performance

[2516] The benefits that lie in the fact that new technology simplifies many processes and operating routines are constantly being realized by building more and more individually simpler components into more complex and complicated systems with correspondingly higher performance

[2517] This increases the demands on the training standards of personnel and departments

[2518] However, high training standards tend to entail high operating costs

[2519] The acquisition of high-tech equipment will subsequently also lead to operating costs that will rarely, if ever, be lower than those of the equipment being replaced

[2520] Consequences for the consideration of balance in the defense organization

[2521] The outcome of a military conflict with modern weapons fought according to a modern operational concept will be highly sensitive to deficiencies or imbalances between the parties in critical sectors

[2522] The connections between the individual combat functions are very clear, and weaknesses in one field can easily be amplified through the consequences it has for other parts of the battle

[2523] For example, loss of air control could dramatically weaken the naval and land forces' ability to conduct effective defensive combat, and the inability to coordinate combat will greatly reduce the impact of weapons that are already very effective

[2524] This means that there is little point in developing sectors of the defense or of a single branch of defense at the expense of others on which the prioritized elements depend in order to function effectively

[2525] Consequences for military strategy

[2526] The development of effective long-range weapons increases the possibilities of using military force to advance one's own interests without resorting to invasion and occupation of the opponent's territory

[2527] A militarily technologically advanced state will be able to subjugate a less advanced adversary politically by threatening with precision-guided conventional weapons that can destroy energy supplies, communications, industry and other infrastructure with relatively minimal loss of human life

[2528] Technological developments have thus contributed to making military power a more flexible political instrument

[2529] However, militarily-technologically equivalent states or groupings of countries will not be able to employ such a strategy

[2530] The risk of mutual destruction could then be far too high, not least because militarily and technologically advanced societies would also be economically and industrially vulnerable

[2531] As a result of the new international situation and the absence of the old East/West divide, the United States, based on its previous SDI (Strategic Defense Initiative) program, is developing the so-called Global Protection Against Limited Strikes (GPALS) program

[2532] This is a long-term research program designed to clarify the possibilities and possibly develop the necessary technology to establish effective defense systems against the regional use of ballistic missiles and weapons of mass destruction
